abstract: Current lipid nanoparticle (LNP) optimisation and quality control frameworks suffer from a common limitation: they treat LNP formulations as morphologically uniform systems, obscuring single-particle structural heterogeneity. This opinion piece challenges the historical misconception that non-spherical, blebbed LNP architectures represent accidental manufacturing artefacts. Instead, we propose that the deliberate engineering of these non-equilibrium architectures represents a game-changing paradigm shift in RNA therapeutics. Consolidating emerging performance data, we argue that blebbed subpopulations yield enhancements in both in vitro and in vivo transfection potency. Blebbed LNPs may confer a particular advantage in difficult-to-transfect immune cell populations, thereby expanding their potential applications in immunotherapy and vaccine development. Mechanistically, this superior performance is proposed to be driven by the thermodynamic sequestration of ribonucleic acid (RNA) within the aqueous bleb compartment, shielding it from lipidation and degradation. Furthermore, we outline how bleb fraction can be prospectively engineered as a target product quality attribute using early-stage thermodynamic levers, specifically high-molarity kosmotropic buffers and delayed kinetic quenching under symmetric mixing conditions. To transition these architectures into a scalable clinical reality, we present a multi-parametric analytical roadmap combining automated, AI-enabled image analysis (LNP-MOD), cryogenic chemical mapping (Cryo-ToF-SIMS), high-resolution fractionation (AF4-SAXS), and single-particle loading quantification (NanoFCM, CLiC-ALEX). Crucially, we call for this analytical framework to be paired with biological validation across clinically relevant cell lines, prioritising immune cell populations to map subpopulation-specific trafficking. Ultimately, we advocate that specifying controlled morphological heterogeneity as a Critical Quality Attribute (CQA) managed during the manufacturing, storage and distribution stages is a true game-changer for the field. This framework has the potential to enable greater therapeutic potency, improve shelf-life, while also broadening global access to next-generation RNA medicine by reducing some of the logistical barriers often encountered in resource-limited settings.

title: Engineering and Analytics of Blebbed Lipid Nanoparticles for Next-Generation RNA Therapeutics.

abstract: mRNA vaccines established scalable manufacturing and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery for sequence-defined, non-integrating RNA medicines. In vivo CAR-T therapy repurposes this platform to generate CAR-positive lymphocytes after intravenous dosing, but its active product is a time-varying cell population rather than the injected RNA mass. This review critically examines the pharmacological sequence from biodistribution and cell-specific uptake to cytosolic RNA release, surface CAR expression, effector function, and disease response. The evidence comprises primary human T cells, mice, humanized mice, non-human primates, and 11 patients described in one correspondence and two meeting abstracts (as of July 2026). Matched studies show that receptor internalization can outweigh surface abundance, ligand density follows a non-monotonic relationship with delivery, and lipid chemistry and ligand presentation independently alter productive T-cell transfection. Preclinical models demonstrate transient CAR expression and target-cell depletion, whereas current human reports establish feasibility but not durable efficacy, a dose-response relationship, or the incidence of uncommon toxicities. We therefore distinguish administered dose, cell-resolved CAR-positive-cell exposure, and pharmacodynamic response, and propose their joint measurement as the basis for comparing platforms and selecting repeat-dose regimens.

title: From mRNA Vaccines to In Vivo CAR-T Therapy: RNA-LNP Design and the Pharmacology of CAR-Positive Cells.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have emerged as a powerful vaccination platform, yet efficient and targeted delivery of mRNA to professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) remains a major challenge. Here, we developed a dendritic cell (DC)-targeting virus-like particle (DVLP) platform for mRNA delivery by combining human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) Gag fused with the bacteriophage MS2 coat protein, which recognizes mRNA bearing MS2 stem-loop sequences and an engineered Sindbis virus glycoprotein mutant (SV-Gmt) that preferentially targets dendritic cells. African swine fever virus (ASFV) P30 was employed as a model antigen to evaluate platform performance. In vitro, SV-Gmt-pseudotyped VLPs encapsulating P30 mRNA (DVLP-P30) preferentially delivered antigen mRNA to dendritic cells compared with broad-tropic vesicular stomatitis virus G protein (VSV-G)-pseudotyped VLPs encapsulating P30 mRNA (VSV-G VLP-P30). In mice, vaccination with DVLP-P30 induced significantly higher P30-specific antibody responses than VSV-G VLP-P30. Enhanced humoral immunity was accompanied by increased frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ effector memory T cells, indicating improved generation of antigen-specific immune memory. Notably, DC-targeted mRNA delivery promoted stronger interferon-γ responses and increased IgG2a production, consistent with a Type 1 helper T cell (Th1)-skewed immune profile. Together, these findings demonstrate that DC-targeting VLPs function as effective mRNA carriers and enhance both the magnitude and quality of vaccine-induced immunity. This work establishes a versatile platform for targeted mRNA delivery and supports further development of DVLPs for prophylactic and therapeutic vaccination.

title: Dendritic cell-targeting virus-like particles as mRNA carriers induce Th1-skewed humoral and cellular immunity.

abstract: Introduction: Next-generation malaria vaccines are urgently needed to provide greater efficacy and longevity. Antibodies targeting blood-stage merozoites can confer protection against clinical malaria through multiple Fc-mediated functions. In particular, merozoite surface protein 2 (PfMSP2) is a known target of protective antibodies that can clear merozoites via multiple antibody Fc-mediated functions, making it a highly promising vaccine candidate. Methods: We developed PfMSP2 as a self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine, which was successfully validated for in vitro expression in mammalian cells. Subsequently, the PfMSP2-saRNA was formulated as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and evaluated for immunogenicity in mice following a three-dose regimen comparing 1 μg and 10 μg doses. We evaluated the induction of antibodies with functional activities relevant to protective immunity. Results: Our PfMSP2-saRNA vaccine induced antigen-specific IgG responses that recognised the surface of whole merozoites. Both 1 μg and 10 μg dosing regimens induced comparable antibodies to PfMSP2, and responses were predominantly murine cytophilic IgG subclasses. These vaccine-induced antibodies demonstrated potent Fc-mediated functions, including complement fixation and binding of human Fcγ-receptor I (FcγRI), after only two doses, which remained consistent after the third dose. Conclusions: PfMSP2 is highly immunogenic using the saRNA vaccine platform in a potential dose-sparing regimen, and induces antibodies with multiple Fc-mediated functions associated with protective immunity in humans. This saRNA platform is a promising strategy to develop highly efficacious vaccines requiring lower and fewer doses.

title: Evaluating a Potential Dose-Sparing Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccine for Induction of Functional Antibodies to Blood-Stage Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics represent a transformative pharmacological paradigm in which the delivery vehicle, genetic payload, and expressed protein form a tightly coupled system. This multicomponent structure introduces nonlinear, multiscale dynamics that challenge traditional pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic frameworks, making quantitative modeling essential.
AREAS COVERED: This review provides a structured biological framework for mRNA-LNP therapeutics, detailing the key processes governing delivery, endosomal escape, mRNA stability, and translation, and highlighting their associated temporal and spatial scales, providing the key aspects to consider for modeling. Building on this foundation, we summarize mathematical modeling approaches, including pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK), and quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models, used to represent these mechanisms. The literature was surveyed to identify representative preclinical and translational studies, focusing on model structure, assumptions, and their use in human projection and dose optimization.
EXPERT OPINION: Mathematical models are increasingly critical to interpret and predict mRNA therapeutic behavior, yet challenges remain in parameter identifiability, data availability, and model standardization. Future advances will depend on biologically grounded modeling frameworks, improved integration of mechanistic insight with quantitative approaches, and tighter coupling between experimental design and model development. These developments will support more efficient translation and enable precision medicine applications.

title: Mathematical modeling in mRNA therapeutics: towards a pathway to individualized treatment protocols.

abstract: Therapy resistance in prostate cancer can emerge at different disease stages; castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is one clinically important state, and resistance to individual therapies may overlap but is not synonymous with CRPC. Metabolic reprogramming-including changes in glycolysis, de novo lipogenesis, glutamine metabolism, and mitochondrial homeostasis-has been implicated in prostate cancer progression and treatment resistance, although the strength of evidence varies across pathways and treatment settings. CircRNAs have been reported to modulate selected metabolic nodes in prostate cancer, although direct links between circRNA-associated metabolic changes and acquired therapy resistance are established only in a subset of studies. This review evaluates circRNAs as candidate regulators of selected metabolic processes in therapy-resistant prostate cancer. Mechanistically, individual circRNAs have been associated with selected metabolic changes through proposed miRNA-mediated interactions and, in some reports, peptide translation or protein scaffolding. These metabolic changes could, in principle, intersect with immunometabolic programmes such as lactate-associated suppression, lipid-linked macrophage states, and adenosine signalling; however, direct evidence that individual circRNAs control these immune-cell processes in CRPC remains limited, as detailed in the evidence tiers later in this review. Therapy-specific resistance networks are organised for enzalutamide/androgen deprivation therapy, docetaxel, PARP inhibitors and radiotherapy, distinguishing metabolism-dependent axes from signalling, mitotic, DNA-repair and exosome-propagated routes. Beyond mechanistic insights, circRNAs hold promise as non-invasive liquid-biopsy biomarkers and as druggable targets amenable to antisense oligonucleotide silencing, mimic delivery, and engineered circRNA vaccines. Major barriers to clinical translation include incomplete multi-therapy metabolic maps, sparse stage-resolved evidence across the hormone-sensitive→CRPC→neuroendocrine continuum, and unresolved delivery, safety, and regulatory challenges. Overall, current evidence supports circRNA-associated metabolic vulnerabilities as a promising preclinical research framework; however, circRNA-targeted metabolic interventions for therapy-resistant prostate cancer have not yet been clinically validated.

title: Circular RNAs in metabolic reprogramming and therapy resistance in prostate cancer: emerging links to the tumor immune microenvironment.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines offer a flexible approach to colorectal cancer (CRC) immunotherapy, with applications ranging from postoperative residual disease to metastatic cancer. This narrative review examines antigen selection, RNA engineering, nanodelivery, and clinical development, drawing on literature available through 21 October 2026. Tumor-associated antigens, shared driver mutations, and personalized neoantigens offer different advantages in population coverage, specificity, and manufacturing. Their activity also depends on RNA chemistry and carrier design, including lipid composition, endosomal release, APC targeting, tissue distribution, stability, and repeated dosing. Early clinical studies have demonstrated antigen-specific T-cell responses in selected patients, while randomized melanoma data provide a benchmark for combining vaccination with checkpoint blockade. The termination of the CRC adjuvant autogene cevumeran monotherapy trial highlights the difficulty of translating immune priming into recurrence prevention. Antigen heterogeneity, impaired HLA presentation, stromal exclusion, and liver-associated immune suppression remain important barriers in CRC. Advances in neoantigen prediction, self-amplifying RNA, and mechanism-based combinations may improve vaccine design, but their clinical value will depend on disease-specific trials that account for manufacturing feasibility and established oncological endpoints. The available evidence remains heterogeneous, with small CRC cohorts and limited randomized outcomes; the non-systematic search also introduces potential selection bias.

abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

abstract: Although the FLT3 inhibitor gilteritinib is initially effective in patients with FLT3-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML), patients invariably relapse within months of treatment. Gilteritinib resistance is commonly driven by the emergence of NRAS mutations and a shift toward a more monocytic cell state. We hypothesized that directly targeting and depleting NRAS protein would reverse these adaptive differentiation changes and restore therapeutic sensitivity. To test this, we used a mutation-agnostic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively knock down NRAS expression across gilteritinib-resistant AML cell lines, in vivo cell line-derived xenografts, and primary patient samples. NRAS ASO successfully resensitized gilteritinib-resistant cells with multiple distinct NRAS mutations, displaying superior efficacy compared with downstream MEK inhibition. This therapeutic efficacy was independent of NRAS-mutant variant allele frequency, suggesting that wild-type NRAS may also contribute to resistance. Comprehensive multiomics profiling (transcriptomics, proteomics, and phosphoproteomics) revealed that NRAS knockdown consistently reversed the monocytic phenotype, shifting cells back toward a more primitive cell state. Monocytic differentiation and NRAS mutations are established drivers of resistance to diverse targeted regimens in AML, including FLT3, IDH, and BCL2 inhibitors. Therefore, we also tested venetoclax-resistant primary cells with NRAS mutations. Resistant cells were resensitized to venetoclax after NRAS knockdown, suggesting that NRAS knockdown may be more broadly applicable for overcoming monocytic cell state and drug resistance in AML.

abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.

abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to assess the safety and tolerability of a virus replicon particle (VRP) encapsulated saRNA encoding IL-12 when injected into in head and neck cancer patients. The main questions being addressed are:

The safety and tolerability of intratumoral (IT) injections of VRP-encapsulated saRNA encoding IL-12 (VLPONC-01)

The tumor response to IT injections of VLPONC-01

The tumor response due to the combination of IT injections of VLPONC-01 and system IV administration of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) treatment

Researchers will compare neoadjuvant pembrolizumab alone to the combination therapy to see if the combination enhances tumor responses.

description:
The study is an Open label, Phase I study to determine the safety of IT injected VLPONC-01 as a therapeutic agent in subjects with non-resectable and resectable Head and Neck Cancer Squamous Cell Carcinomas (HCSCC), and secondarily to assess pathologic response and radiological response (assessed by RECIST 1.1 criteria) in the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes. Researchers also will explore tumor microenvironment changes in cytokine levels and cellular responses.

There will be three distinct cohorts enrolling sequentially:

Cohort A: Researchers will enroll unresectable or recurrent/metastatic head and neck cancer with at least 1 injectable tumor not scheduled for tumor resection surgery who will receive four doses of VLPONC-01.

Cohort C: Researchers will enroll HCSCC patients scheduled for tumor resection surgery who will receive four doses of VLPONC-1 and two doses of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab or only two doses of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab prior to tumor resection surgery.

abstract: Cancer remains a leading global mortality cause, driven by complex interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) that facilitate progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Cytokines form the central regulatory network governing TME intercellular communication, exerting highly context-dependent pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects. Dysregulated cytokine signaling drives chronic inflammation and immunosuppression, limiting durable therapeutic responses. While cytokine-based immunotherapies show clinical potential, their widespread use is hindered by poor stability, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and dose-limiting toxicities. Advances in nanomedicine offer innovative solutions by improving cytokine pharmacokinetics, tumor-selective delivery, and spatiotemporally controlled release. Beyond passive delivery, engineered nanoplatforms act as active modulators of the tumor immune ecosystem, remodeling cytokine networks to restore antitumor immunity. Nanotechnology interventions effectively regulate key signaling pathways- including JAK/STAT, TGF-β/SMAD, NF-κB, MAPK/ERK, and PI3K/AKT- disrupting pathological feedback mechanisms and crosstalk. Furthermore, localized cytokine delivery, gene silencing, mRNA therapeutics, and CRISPR-enabled genome engineering are expanding precision immunotherapy. Despite significant translational challenges such as tumor heterogeneity, biological barriers, immunogenicity, and manufacturing complexity emerging biomimetic and personalized nanoplatforms offer promising avenues for precise immune modulation and biomarker-guided patient stratification. Literature searches were conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect (with Google Scholar for citation tracking) covering peer-reviewed publications from 2003 to 2026.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mRNA vaccines compressed the path from pathogen sequence to licensed product into less than a year and are now approved for three viral diseases (COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus and seasonal influenza), with more than twenty indications in clinical development. The platform's potency is no longer in doubt; its predictability is. We argue that progress is now limited by three interfaces that are engineered largely independently: the lipid-RNA interface, which sets encapsulation, internal structure and storage stability; the particle-cell interface, which sets tropism and the efficiency of endosomal escape; and the particle-immune interface, which sets the balance between adjuvanticity and reactogenicity. Quantitative design rules exist for the first interface, remain empirical for the second, and are almost absent for the third, which is why formulation development still proceeds by screening rather than by calculation. We review the molecular design of the mRNA payload and structural antigen selection; the chemistry, manufacture and intracellular trafficking of LNPs; the immunological chain that links innate activation and dendritic-cell cross-presentation to germinal-centre output; and the clinical evidence across COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, cytomegalovirus, HIV, personalised cancer vaccines and other targets. We conclude by identifying the measurements, pharmacopoeial quality attributes and design rules that would make the next generation of LNP-mRNA vaccines predictable rather than empirical.

abstract: A biomimetic magnetic nanocarrier was developed to facilitate the targeted delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 components to breast cancer cells, with the aim of improving tumor-directed gene delivery and reducing nonspecific distribution to healthy tissues. The effective delivery vector for partial WT1 disruption consists of a superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle (SPION) core loaded with a genome-editing plasmid. The SPION is wrapped in a red blood cell membrane functionalized with the nuclear- and cancer cell-targeting aptamer AS1411. Findings from cytotoxicity assays and western blot analyses validated the effectiveness of this delivery system. Furthermore, fluorescence imaging and flow cytometry demonstrated enhanced GFP reporter expression in 4T1 cells treated with PSMA compared with the nontargeted formulation, suggesting improved functional plasmid delivery. In vivo investigations revealed substantial tumor-growth inhibition following PSMA administration, while ex vivo fluorescence imaging showed enhanced tumor-associated GFP reporter signals compared with the nontargeted formulation. Moreover, the diagnostic potential of the synthesized SPION-CRISPR/Cas9 plasmid/membrane/aptamer complex was evaluated using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which revealed enhanced contrast at the tumor site. Overall, this platform demonstrates potential for tumor-directed plasmid delivery and MRI-based imaging, although further studies are required to establish reproducible WT1-editing efficiency, long-term safety, and therapeutic specificity.

title: Biomimetic magnetic nanocarriers for theranostic CRISPR/Cas9 delivery: targeting WT1 in a murine model of breast cancer.

abstract: One approach to therapeutic cancer vaccine development uses whole tumor cells or their lysates as sources of a broad repertoire of tumor antigens. A key advantage of this strategy is that it does not require prior identification of tumor antigens, unlike personalized neoantigen peptide or mRNA vaccines, potentially reducing the time and cost of vaccine development. However, late-phase clinical trials have not demonstrated sufficient efficacy of tumor cell-based cancer vaccines. Currently, strategies to enhance the therapeutic potential of vaccines based on whole tumor cells and their derived lysates are being actively developed, and the vaccine potential of individual tumor cell components, such as cell membranes and extracellular vesicles, is under investigation. In this review, we systematize data on how whole tumor cells and their derivatives (lysates, cell membranes, and extracellular vesicles) are used to generate therapeutic cancer vaccines, analyze the results of experimental and clinical studies, and evaluate promising engineering and combination therapy strategies capable of overcoming the current limitations of this platform.

abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) is a key reproductive barrier in citrus species that prevents self-fertilization and maintains genetic diversity. In pummelo (Citrus grandis L. Osbeck), SI is governed by an S-ribonuclease (S-RNase)-based gametophytic system, but the mechanisms underlying pollen tube rejection remain poorly understood. Here, we identified pollen-expressed arginine decarboxylase (ADC) as a non-S-locus factor that interacts with S-RNases and may contribute to pollen tube responses under S-RNase-associated stress. Phylogenetic and structural analyses indicated that CgADC belongs to the conserved plant arginine decarboxylase family. Molecular docking predicted a potential hydrophobic interaction interface between CgADC and S-RNase. Using yeast two-hybrid screening, split-luciferase complementation, pull-down assays, and subcellular localization, we found that CgADC associates with multiple S-haplotype S-RNases. CgADC transcripts were significantly more abundant under incompatible conditions, while recombinant CgADC exhibited enhanced enzymatic activity following S-RNase treatment in vitro. Antisense oligonucleotide-mediated suppression of CgADC expression significantly reduced pollen tube elongation. Exogenous recombinant CgADC partially alleviated pollen tube growth inhibition and was associated with changes in ROS-related fluorescence patterns. However, its uptake into the pollen tube cytoplasm was not directly demonstrated. Together, these findings identify CgADC as a potential non-S-locus factor associated with the pummelo SI response and suggest a link between S-RNase-associated responses, ADC activity, and ROS-related regulation.

abstract: Transient RNA delivery offers a practical approach to programmable genome editing without introducing editor-encoding DNA, but editing performance depends on reagent design, delivery conditions, and target accessibility. Here, we evaluated an RNA-based editing workflow built around a cytosine base editor derived from targeted activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID)-mediated mutagenesis (TAM). Systematic adjustment of editor mRNA and guide RNA dosage, poly(A) tail configuration, and untranslated regions identified parameters influencing cytosine-to-thymine conversion; viability remained high at 24 h under the tested RNA-dose conditions. Further optimized electroporation enabled efficient reporter mRNA delivery into primary human CD8+ T cells. In two independent donor experiments, targeted nucleotide conversion at the endogenous CD3E locus and the CD3-negative fraction were higher after sequential than after single electroporation. To investigate splice-site editing, we screened AID-Cas9 combinations targeting the mouse Nr4a2 exon 3 splice acceptor and generated mutant mice through embryo editing and subsequent breeding. Sanger sequencing of genomic DNA from primary CD8+ T cells confirmed the intended Nr4a2 splice-site mutation, while Hi-TOM-based targeted cDNA amplicon sequencing revealed altered splice-junction patterns, including the emergence of an unexpected splice junction in mutant cells. However, no statistically significant differences in tumor progression were detected in the B16-OVA adoptive transfer or B16F10 tumor models. Together, these findings provide a practical framework for transient RNA-based base editing in primary T cells and targeted modification of splice-regulatory sequences, while highlighting the complexity of splice-site editing outcomes.

abstract: mRNA-based cancer vaccines have emerged as a promising platform for therapeutic cancer immunotherapy because of their ability to encode tumor-associated antigens, tumor-specific antigens, and patient-specific neoantigens and to induce antigen-specific immune responses. Their flexible and cell-free manufacturing enables rapid adaptation and facilitates the development of personalized vaccines based on individual tumor mutations and HLA profiles. However, the clinical translation of mRNA-based cancer vaccines remains challenging because of difficulties in neoantigen identification, maintaining mRNA stability, achieving efficient intracellular and tissue-specific delivery and endosomal escape, optimizing antigen expression, and overcoming tumor heterogeneity, and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments. Advances in mRNA engineering, including sequence optimization, modified nucleosides, cap and UTR optimization, and lipid nanoparticle-based delivery, have improved RNA stability, cellular uptake, antigen expression, and immune activation in various experimental and clinical settings. This review discusses the principles of mRNA-based cancer vaccines, strategies for neoantigen identification and vaccine development, mRNA production and formulation, nanoparticle-mediated delivery, major challenges affecting stability, targeting, expression, and immune stimulation, and emerging clinical applications. Particular emphasis is placed on personalized neoantigen vaccines and combination approaches with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Continued integration of RNA engineering, nanotechnology, computational antigen prediction, and precision immunotherapy may enable more effective and clinically adaptable mRNA-based cancer vaccines.

abstract: Maternal messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccination can generate maternal immunity and antibodies for passive infant protection. However, clinical evidence derives predominantly from the SARS-CoV-2 vaccines BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273, limiting generalization across the platform. This narrative review examines three questions: what determines maternal immune responses, what governs placental antibody transfer, and how immunological findings relate to infant clinical protection. Studies generally support preserved immune responsiveness during pregnancy, but associations with gestational timing are difficult to separate from dose number, previous infection, and time since antigen exposure. Transfer requires interpretation of maternal and cord-blood concentrations, because high transfer ratios do not necessarily indicate high infant antibody levels. Postnatal antibody decline and variant-dependent neutralization further limit inference from measurements at delivery. Observational studies associate maternal vaccination with reduced COVID-19-associated infant hospitalization, although residual confounding and heterogeneous exposure histories complicate comparisons between schedules. No validated infant antibody threshold predicts protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection or hospitalization. Evidence for other pathogens and self-amplifying RNA remains predominantly preclinical. Maternal immunogenicity, placental transfer, and antibody persistence therefore provide complementary evidence but cannot substitute for clinical outcomes. Future products require pregnancy-specific safety assessment and prospective studies linking maternal responses, functional antibody transfer, and postnatal persistence to clinically meaningful protection throughout infancy.

outcomes.description: Questionnaire to document solicited reactions is developed specifically for this study. Data will be reported as the proportion of participants who report by each intervention arm. Solicited reactions such as pain, tenderness, erythema/redness, induration/swelling, fever, nausea/vomiting, headache, fatigue/malaise, myalgia, arthralgia will be collected from the participants 7 days post-vaccination. Reactogenicity was graded on a 0-4 scale: Grade 0 = no symptom; Grade 1 = mild and does not interfere with activity; Grade 2 = moderate or requiring repeated non-narcotic analgesia; Grade 3 = severe, limiting or preventing daily activity; Grade 4 = potentially life-threatening, requiring ER visit or hospitalisation.

abstract: Plant genome editing has been limited by the difficulty of delivering CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) reagents to germline-competent cells without stable transgene integration. Viral vectors address this by exploiting endogenous replication, cell-to-cell movement and phloem transport, but cargo capacity and germline access have so far traded against each other. We classify virus-induced genome editing (VIGE) systems along two binary design choices: whether the vector itself encodes the nuclease and whether an engineered mobility mechanism carries the editing reagents to the germline. These two axes define four delivery architectures: (a) guide-only without a mobility element, in which guides are delivered into a nuclease-expressing host; (b) guide-only with a mobile RNA element that carries the guide into meristematic cells, yielding heritable edits without tissue culture; (c) nuclease-encoding without a route to the germline, achieved by shrinking the nuclease or enlarging the vector; and (d) nuclease-encoding with a mobility element, reaching the germline directly. We evaluate all four architectures against three persistent constraints. These are off-target risks from viral amplification of the editing reagents, the host range of the available vectors, and the gap between model-system demonstrations and breeding pipelines. Finally, we propose that combining engineered compact nucleases, mobile RNA signals, and morphogenic regulators could enable a single-vector pipeline for producing edited seeds. This would extend genome editing to refractory crop species and reduce reliance on tissue-culture-based transformation.

description:
This is a Phase II, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of NWRD09 in patients with HPV16 positive cervical high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). Eligible participants are randomized to receive either NWRD09 or the corresponding placebo.

Participants will receive intramuscular injections of either NWRD09 or matching placebo at the corresponding dose at weeks 0, 2, 4, and 12 (a total of 4 doses).

Efficacy evaluations at Week 24 will include histopathological biopsy and HPV testing.

abstract: PRE-EMPT will assemble a cohort of 150 participants from three populations (low risk, intermediate risk, and high risk for self-harm). We will obtain clinical assessments, structural and functional MRI utilizing tasks pioneered by our team to assess cognitive control (CC) and emotion regulation (ER), and peripheral circular RNA (circRNA) levels to characterize the molecular brain states associated with behavioral risk. The clinical, imaging, and transcriptomic data will be fused and jointly analyzed to increase the accuracy of our risk prediction models. PRE-EMPT in three separate Aims will then prospectively assess three promising and innovative interventions for their potential to reduce suicidal ideation and alter activity in key neural networks: 1) neurofeedback (NF) using real-time fMRI with simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG), 2) a form of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) called accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (aiTBS) with dose optimization through electric field modeling; and 3) psilocybin assisted therapy (PSI), with flexible dosing plan to maximize the depth of psychedelic experience. These therapies were chosen based on our team's prior work in all three interventions demonstrating rapid action and large effects.

outcomes.description: Aim 1 will recruit a low risk to intermediate risk populations, i.e., low-to-moderate levels of depression or anxiety/PTSD with occasional suicidal ideation, up to significant depression and anxiety with chronic suicidal ideation). Following baseline assessment with the universal assessment battery, participants will be randomized to active or sham group and undergo real-time fMRI neurofeedback studies occurring across two visits.
outcomes.measure: Neurofeedback
outcomes.time_frame: From enrollment through post-treatment visit about 6-8 weeks.

outcomes.description: Aim 2 will recruit an intermediate to high risk population (i.e., significant depression and anxiety; chronic suicidal ideation) to receive aiTBS, an efficient FDA-cleared form of rTMS for major depressive disorder
outcomes.measure: TMS
outcomes.time_frame: From enrollment through post-treatment visit about 6-8 weeks.

outcomes.description: Aim 3 will administer psilocybin assisted therapy in intermediate and high risk patients to reduce suicidal ideation and identify mediators of response. Participants will receive two separate psilocybin sessions accompanied by preparation and integration therapy. Factors such as dose, depression severity, serotonergic use, and depth of mystical experiences will be correlated with suicidality reduction.
outcomes.measure: Psilocybin
outcomes.time_frame: From enrollment through post-treatment visit about 6-8 weeks.

outcomes.description: Aim 4 will combine clinical, imaging, and circular RNA data gathered across Aims 1, 2, and 3 at baseline into a predictive model for behavioral risk and suicidal ideation. Co-I Plis will use joint information, dynamic connectivity, and deep learning to enhance prediction of behavioral risk. Circular RNA data from Co-I Cruchaga will be fused with the imaging and clinical data.
outcomes.measure: Predictive model
outcomes.time_frame: From enrollment through post-treatment visit about 6-8 weeks.

abstract:
The Investigators have demonstrated in preclinical studies that RNA liposomes activate APCs, induce antigen-specific T cell immunity, and can supplant DCs in a cell therapy model for HGG and have shown feasibility and activity of this approach in preclinical models and in canine patients with a spontaneous malignant glioma. In one arm of this study, the investigators investigate the safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccines in pediatric patients with recurrent pHGG.

The investigators have also shown that intravenous administration of tumor mRNA loaded lipid particles (LPs) localizes primarily to lung, transfect antigen presenting cells (APCs) and lead to an activated T cell response for induction of anti-tumor immunity. In contrast to other formulations, RNA-LPs recruit multiple arms of the immune system (i.e. innate/adaptive), and remodel the systemic/intratumoral immune milieu, which remain potent barriers for vaccine, cellular, and checkpoint inhibiting immunotherapies. The investigators have already demonstrated safety of RNA-LPs in acute/chronic murine toxicity studies, and in client-owned canine trial.

In this study, the investigators will investigate the manufacturing feasibility, safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccine in patients with recurrent pulmonary or unresectable osteosarcoma and recurrent pHGG.

description:
For recurrent pHGG there will be two non-randomized arms assigned at the discretion of the patient and treatment team:

* Arm 1-A single neoadjuvant pp65 RNA-LP (DP1) will be administered prior to surgical resection/biopsy, and then two adjuvant DP1.
* Arm 2-Surgical resection/biopsy will occur first and all three DP1 will be administered in the adjuvant setting

The Phase I dose-escalation study for recurrent/progressive pHGG cohort will be performed in 18 subjects using a 3+3 design. Both recurrent pHGG trial arms will be enrolled together as a single cohort for safety.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapy offers a programmable route to melanoma treatment, but its translation is limited by nuclease degradation, off-target biodistribution and endolysosomal trapping. Here we report a glutathione (GSH)/pH dual-responsive mRNA nanocomplex (mRNA-NC) fabricated by one-pot in situ polymerization of N-(3-aminopropyl)methacrylamide (APMA), 1-vinylimidazole (VI), N,N'-bis(acryloyl)cystamine (BACA), and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine (MPC) on the mRNA template. At an N/P ratio of 40, the carrier reached an encapsulation efficiency of 92.7 ± 2.1% and a loading capacity of 87.4 ± 3.2 μg mg-1, forming monodisperse particles of 126.4 ± 7.2 nm (polydispersity index, PDI, 0.14). The zwitterionic corona limited plasma protein adsorption to 12.6 ± 1.5 μg mg-1 (4.6-fold lower than jetPEI/mRNA), kept hemolysis at 0.8 ± 0.2%, and extended the serum half-life of the mRNA to ≈27.4 h, roughly 9-fold longer than naked mRNA. Release was gated by both triggers: 86.5 ± 3.7% of the cargo was released within 8 h under 10 mM GSH, whereas leakage under physiological conditions remained ≤ 12%; in a 4 h matrix, pH 5.5 plus 10 mM GSH released 85 ± 6.8% versus 12 ± 1.5% at pH 7.4 without GSH. In B16F10 cells, the nanocomplex was taken up in a dose- and energy-dependent manner, entered the lysosomal compartment, and escaped over time in a manner consistent with imidazole-mediated proton-sponge buffering (a hypothesis; intralysosomal pH was not measured directly), producing a peak firefly luciferase (FLuc) expression of 56,140 ± 3280 RLU mg-1 protein at 24 h, about 1.5-fold higher than jetPEI/mRNA, with 93.6 ± 3.9% cell viability and 6.7 ± 1.2% lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release. In B16F10-bearing albino C57BL/6 mice, a single intravenous dose produced tumor-dominant bioluminescence (peak 5.7 × 106 photons s-1 at 6 h), a tumor enrichment index of 1.22 ± 0.18 (vs 0.31 ± 0.03 for jetPEI/mRNA) and 2.42 × 107 FLuc mRNA copies μg-1 tumor RNA at 12 h, while all 7-day safety indicators remained at phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) levels. These results demonstrate that a single zwitterionic nanocomplex can integrate stealth, dual-triggered release, and endosomal escape for safe, tumor-enriched mRNA delivery. While this study focuses on delivery performance and reporter gene expression, it lays a solid foundation for future therapeutic applications with functional mRNA.

abstract: Diabetes mellitus is characterised by progressive loss or dysfunction of functional β-cell mass arising through distinct but overlapping mechanisms in type 1 and type 2 diabetes, including autoimmune-mediated destruction, metabolic stress, and microenvironmental dysfunction. Despite major advances in pharmacological and technological management, current therapies remain largely compensatory and have not consistently restored endogenous β-cell function. Stem cell-based approaches have therefore emerged as promising strategies to address the underlying pathophysiology of the disease. This review synthesises stem cell-based therapies across four complementary therapeutic components: (1) β-cell replacement through pluripotent stem cell differentiation and emerging platforms such as direct reprogramming and islet organoids; (2) systemic immune modulation or immune resetting via hematopoietic stem cell-based interventions and regulatory immune modulation; (3) local graft protection and microenvironmental repair mediated by mesenchymal stromal cells, extracellular vesicles, and biomaterial-based approaches; and (4) cell-intrinsic immune engineering to reduce immune recognition of transplanted cells. While β-cell replacement strategies have demonstrated significant progress toward generating functional insulin-producing cells, their clinical efficacy remains constrained by incomplete maturation, immune rejection, and limited engraftment. Immune resetting approaches provide mechanistic evidence for the potential reversibility of autoimmune dysfunction but are limited by toxicity and the lack of durable tolerance. In contrast, local paracrine and microenvironmental strategies exert immunomodulatory and cytoprotective effects that stabilise the islet microenvironment but do not directly restore β-cell mass. Cell-intrinsic immune engineering offers an alternative strategy to reduce immune recognition of transplanted cells, although long-term immune evasion, genomic safety, and graft durability remain important translational challenges. These findings indicate that single-modality approaches are unlikely to be sufficient to achieve durable disease modification. Instead, effective therapeutic strategies may require integrated, multi-axis interventions that combine β-cell replacement, immune modulation, and microenvironmental support. Emerging advances in genome engineering, biomaterial-based encapsulation, and extracellular vesicle engineering are likely to facilitate this transition toward coordinated regenerative therapies. This integrated framework provides a systems-level perspective on current limitations and future directions for stem cell-based treatment of diabetes mellitus.

abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4-8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA.

abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.

title: A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target.

abstract: Heterobifunctional proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) enable degradation of disease-relevant proteins but have largely been limited to cytosolic targets. Using reporter cell lines and the dTAG system to recruit cytosolic E3 ligases, we found that luminal substrates are resistant to degradation, whereas ER membrane proteins are efficiently degraded across multiple topologies. CRISPR screens confirmed dependence on cullin-RING ligases but did not identify canonical ER-associated degradation (ERAD) components, except the AAA ATPase VCP. Combined loss of DERL1/2/3 and depletion of HRD1 did not impair degradation, further supporting independence from canonical ERAD machinery. Mechanistic studies showed that ubiquitination is required for VCP binding and that removal of ubiquitin chains releases VCP, suggesting direct extraction of ubiquitinated substrates. An atorvastatin-cereblon PROTAC induced VCP-dependent degradation of HMGCR, preventing its compensatory accumulation during statin treatment. Together, these findings support a model in which ubiquitination by a cytosolic E3 ligase is sufficient to engage VCP and drive extraction, potentially bypassing canonical ERAD machinery.

title: Induced ubiquitination drives ER protein degradation through a VCP-dependent pathway.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Telomerase activity is primarily controlled by expression of the catalytic subunit hTERT, yet the mechanisms coordinating its transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation remain incompletely understood. Paradoxically, hypermethylation of a CpG-rich region upstream of the hTERT transcription start site, termed the TERT Hypermethylated Oncological Region (THOR), is strongly associated with hTERT activation. Recent evidence suggests that THOR methylation influences the expression of hTAPAS, a long non-coding RNA transcribed antisense to the hTERT promoter that represses hTERT expression. Here, we investigated the relationship between DNA methylation and alternative splicing of hTERT.
RESULTS: Using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated targeted enrichment combined with Nanopore sequencing, we generated high-resolution DNA methylation maps across several kilobases surrounding the hTERT promoter and intronic regions encompassing exons 6-8 in multiple human cell lines. These analyses identified distinct methylation signatures associated with specific hTERT splice isoform profiles. Functional perturbation experiments further demonstrated that altering the epigenetic state of the hTERT locus influences alternative splicing. Overexpression of the antisense long non-coding RNA hTAPAS, as well as treatment with the DNA demethylating agent 5'-azacytidine, reduced CpG methylation at the hTERT promoter and altered the distribution of hTERT splice isoforms. These findings indicate an association among hTAPAS expression, DNA methylation at the hTERT locus, and hTERT splice isoform profiles.
CONCLUSIONS: Our results identify an association between DNA methylation patterns at the hTERT locus and alternative hTERT splicing and further implicate hTAPAS expression in this regulatory context. These results support an epigenetic mechanism linking hTAPAS to hTERT promoter methylation and splice isoform selection, providing new insight into how telomerase regulation may be remodeled during development and cancer.

title: The lncRNA hTAPAS within the epigenetic landscape of hTERT transcription and splicing.

abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the therapeutic landscape of onco-hematology, evolving from historical allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) to modern chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T/NK cell therapies, bispecific antibodies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors. Central to this immunological cross-talk is the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) system, which governs self/non-self-discrimination, alloreactivity, and tumor immune evasion across both classical allografts and novel adoptive cellular platforms. Facing hematological malignancies, ranging from acute leukemias and multiple myeloma to chronic leukemias and lymphomas, clinicians must overcome tumor immune escape while managing treatment-related toxicities and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GvHD). Advances in high-throughput molecular biology techniques, notably Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) and long-read sequencing, have become indispensable for high-resolution HLA matching, minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring, and chimerism analysis. Furthermore, gene-editing strategies (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9) targeting TRAC, B2M, and CIITA, alongside HLA-E engineering and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technology, are driving the development of universal "off-the-shelf" effector platforms that bypass classic HLA barriers. In this review, we provide a conceptual synthesis of immunotherapeutic paradigms in onco-hematology, highlighting the pivotal role of HLA biology and molecular diagnostics in shaping next-generation personalized cellular therapies.

abstract: RICTOR, a core component of mTORC2, regulates cell survival, proliferation, and cytoskeletal organization. To dissect its role in epithelial cell biology, we generated ten clonal HEK-293T lines with frameshift deletions in the RICTOR gene using paired sgRNAs targeting exon 3. sgRNA efficiency was assessed by TIDE and T7E1 assays, and the two best sgRNAs were selected for deletion induction. Overall, 10 clonal lines with composite deletion were isolated. Complete loss of RICTOR mRNA in these clones was verified by RT-qPCR. Targeted qRT-PCR profiling revealed a consistent molecular signature: downregulation of some mTORC2-associated genes, compensatory upregulation of mTORC1 components (RPTOR, PRAS40) and PRR5, and increased ERK1/2 mRNA and, in most clones, increased ERK1/2 protein and p-ERK2. Proliferation was significantly slowed (doubling time increased nearly 50%, from 30 to 47 h). Scratch-wound assays demonstrated markedly reduced migration. Notably, RICTOR-KO cells formed compact multicellular aggregates instead of a dispersed monolayer, accompanied by upregulation of adhesion genes (CDH1, FLNA, FN1, ITGA5) and downregulation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers (VIM, SNAI1, ZEB1). Our results establish HEK-293T RICTOR-KO as a valuable model to study mTORC2-dependent regulation of adhesion and migration, and highlight the interplay between mTOR and MAPK signaling in maintaining epithelial homeostasis. Potential therapeutic use of RICTOR-KO as an inhibitor of malignancy of solid tumors deserves further investigation.

abstract: The purpose of this pragmatic randomized trials is to evaluate the comparative vaccine effectiveness (cVE) of mCombriax® (mRNA-1083) versus same day co-administration of the active comparators (i.e., high-dose influenza vaccine/Efluelda® and mRNA-1273/Spikevax®) among adults aged 65 years and older.

description: This Phase 4 randomized, active-comparator, pragmatic trial is designed to evaluate the effectiveness of a seasonal variant-containing formulation of mCombriax® (mRNA-1083) compared with same-day co-administration of authorized standalone enhanced influenza and COVID-19 vaccines in adults aged ≥65 years. The trial is designed to be conducted over two consecutive respiratory virus seasons to account for potential seasonal variation in virus circulation, vaccine composition, and effectiveness. The primary objective is to evaluate the comparative vaccine effectiveness (cVE) of the combination vaccine with respect to clinically relevant outcomes, including severe influenza and COVID-19. Demonstration of non-inferior protection in real-world setting, in combination with the potential programmatic advantages of a single-dose strategy, may support policy recommendations, reimbursement decisions, and broader implementation of combined seasonal respiratory vaccination strategies.

abstract: Obesity is a multifactorial chronic disease associated with chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and gut microbiota dysbiosis. Adipose tissue dysfunction and inflammation may contribute to insulin resistance and metabolic complications and may influence outcomes following bariatric surgery. Synbiotics and probiotics may improve metabolic homeostasis by modulating gut microbiota and inflammatory pathways. However, their potential effects on adipose tissue function before bariatric surgery remain insufficiently investigated. This study aims to evaluate whether 12 weeks of synbiotic supplementation in women with severe obesity scheduled for sleeve gastrectomy can reduce markers of inflammation and endoplasmic reticulum stress. The study will also assess its effects on body weight and metabolic parameters before and after surgery.

abstract: This is an Investigator-initiated, Open-Label Clinical Study of a mRNA Vaccine Encoding Tumor-Specific Circular RNA Antigens in Combination with anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody in Patients with Advanced Solid Tumors. Preclinical studies of this project have identified that circFAM53B, which is specifically overexpressed in tumor cells, possesses the ability to encode a cryptic peptide, FAM53B-219aa, representing a potential tumor vaccine target. In this study, the sequence encoding the cryptic antigen from circFAM53B will be linearized and formulated as an mRNA vaccine (circFAM53B mRNA injection). The vaccine will be administered via lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulation, and its safety and efficacy will be evaluated in combination with anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody therapy.

description:
This investigator-initiated clinical trial is designed to evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of the circFAM53B mRNA vaccine in combination with anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody therapy using a "3+3" dose-escalation design. The trial consists of two phases: a dose-escalation phase and a dose-expansion phase.

In the dose-escalation phase, patients with advanced solid tumors exhibiting high circFAM53B-219aa expression who have failed prior standard therapies will be enrolled. Approximately 10-20 participants will receive the circFAM53B mRNA vaccine to determine the safety profile (DLT) and identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD).

Based on the results from the dose-escalation phase, the dose-expansion phase will be conducted at the identified MTD. This phase will enroll participants from two different tumor types, with approximately 10 patients per cohort, to receive the circFAM53B mRNA vaccine in combination with toripalimab.

abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are increasingly implicated in cancer treatment resistance, but the strength of evidence differs markedly among reported candidates. Because recent reviews have already catalogued circRNA biology, resistance mechanisms, and therapeutic applications, this narrative review focuses on how directly individual findings are linked to response to a defined anticancer treatment. Evidence is interpreted at four levels: human treatment-response data, direct in vivo resistance models, direct resistant cell-line models, and resistance-relevant biology without direct treatment testing. Direct treatment-resistance evidence includes circAKT3 in cisplatin resistance, hsa_circ_0007919 in gemcitabine resistance, circCDYL2 (hsa_circ_0004087) in trastuzumab resistance, and circRNA-SORE in sorafenib resistance. Experimental checkpoint-blockade studies also implicate circFGFR1 and circIGF2BP3 in reduced anti-PD-1 efficacy, although direct therapeutic resensitization by selective inhibition of these circRNAs was not established in the cited experiments. By contrast, several proposed links involving DNA repair, metabolism, stemness, or ferroptosis remain biologically plausible but have not been validated as treatment-resistance mechanisms. This distinction also changes biomarker interpretation: most tissue- or extracellular-vesicle-associated circRNAs should currently be regarded as candidate biomarkers of treatment response rather than clinically validated predictive biomarkers. We summarize the available human evidence, analytical requirements, and potential uses of longitudinal monitoring. Therapeutically, back-splice-junction-specific small interfering RNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, and RNA-targeting CRISPR systems can in principle suppress endogenous resistance-promoting circRNAs, whereas replacement approaches may restore sensitizing circRNAs. These endogenous-targeting strategies remain predominantly preclinical, whereas engineered circRNA therapeutics and cancer vaccines constitute a distinct platform that has begun early clinical development. Because the evidence base is dominated by preclinical models and small or retrospective clinical cohorts, with heterogeneous assays and endpoints, no circRNA discussed here should yet be considered a clinically validated predictive biomarker or an established resistance-reversal target.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: PIKFYVE deficiency has been implicated in congenital cataract, and gene therapy based on PIKFYVE mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) represents a potential therapeutic strategy.
METHODS: We developed an SM-102-based LNP delivery system encapsulating human PIKFYVE mRNA with a long coding sequence, thereby overcoming the payload capacity limitations of conventional viral vectors. To evaluate this LNP system, we identified differentially expressed lysosomal genes via RNA sequencing and investigated its biocompatibility, transfection efficiency, and capacity to rescue lysosomal defects in PIKFYVE knockout lens epithelial cells (PIKFYVE-/-SRA01/04). Additionally, in vivo localized expression was assessed using firefly luciferase (FLuc) mRNA-LNPs administered via subconjunctival, intracameral, intravitreal, and subretinal injections in female C57BL/6J mice.
RESULTS: The mRNA-LNP system exhibited high cytocompatibility and over 99% transfection efficiency in vitro. Treatment dose-dependently increased expression of PIKFYVE, partially rescuing lysosome-related transcripts and attenuating vacuolization in PIKFYVE-/-SRA01/04 cells. This functional restoration enabled the deficient cells to regain a nearly normal morphology, with the intracellular vacuolar area reduced from 14.29% to 7.98%. Furthermore, in vivo imaging demonstrated localized FLuc expression upon mRNA-LNP delivery across four ocular administration routes.
DISCUSSION: This study demonstrates that the PIKFYVE mRNA SM-102-LNP delivery system effectively restores protein expression and rescues lysosomal dysfunction in PIKFYVE-/-SRA01/04 cells. LNP-mediated mRNA replacement represents a practicable, translatable strategy for PIKFYVE-associated cataracts.
CONCLUSION: We constructed a PIKFYVE mRNA-LNP platform that restored protein expression, ameliorated lysosomal dysregulation, and significantly improved cellular morphology. These findings provide a proof-of-concept for an mRNA-LNP therapeutic approach to ophthalmic disorders.

title: Efficient Delivery of PIKFYVE mRNA-LNPs Rescues Lysosomal Dysfunction in PIKFYVE Knockout Lens Epithelial Cells.

abstract: Reactivation of silenced wild-type alleles on the inactive X chromosome (Xi) offers a promising therapeutic avenue for X-linked disorders affecting females. The long non-coding RNA XIST is central to Xi silencing, yet its complete loss risks chromosome-wide dosage imbalance. To explore reactivation in a translational context, we employed chimeric mouse-human FRG livers repopulated with primary hepatocytes from a female patient with ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency exhibiting highly skewed X-inactivation. Adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 delivery was used to disrupt XIST in vivo to assess effects on chromatin landscape and OTC expression. Despite differential XIST promoter methylation, the Xi remained accessible to CRISPR-Cas9, with editing frequencies comparable to those of the active X chromosome. XIST deletion induced limited reactivation of the wild-type OTC allele and was accompanied by broader epigenetic effects. CUT&RUN profiling distinguished effects of vector delivery and XIST deletion, including global H3K4me3 reduction after AAV transduction, X chromosome-restricted H3K27me3 reduction after XIST deletion, and broader H3K27ac reduction in edited hepatocytes. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of manipulating the human Xi in vivo while revealing distinct Xi-specific and broader chromatin effects. Together, they highlight the need for precise, locus-specific strategies to achieve therapeutic gene reactivation while preserving chromosome-wide epigenetic regulation.

title: AAV-mediated XIST deletion in female human hepatocytes with skewed X-inactivation induces limited reactivation of the X-linked OTC gene in vivo.

abstract: Plasmacytoma variant translocation 1 (PVT1), a non-protein coding gene, is overexpressed in aggressive prostate cancer (PCa). Overexpression of PVT1 exon 9 has been demonstrated to induce malignant transformation of prostate epithelial cells and the development of aggressive PCa in vivo. However, the factors regulating overexpression and consequent oncogenicity of PVT1 exon 9 remain unclear. Here, we report the identification and functional characterization of a previously unrecognized internal regulatory element, the PVT1 exon 9 associated promoter (PEAP). We also demonstrate that its activity is governed by the caudal homeobox transcription factor CDX1 and local DNA methylation dynamics. While enzymatic methyl-sequence (EM-seq) profiling of PCa tissues and matched adjacent normal tissues revealed hypomethylation at PEAP in tumors, TFBind-based transcription factor motif prediction analysis revealed a discrete high-affinity CDX1 binding motif within PEAP. Using luciferase reporter assays, siRNA knockdown, CUT&RUN, CRISPR-based perturbation, isoform-specific droplet digital and quantitative PCR, we validated that the CDX1 motif within PEAP is functionally required for PEAP-driven induction of the oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 transcript. Moreover, CDX1 expression was significantly higher in aggressive PCa tissues compared to matched adjacent normal tissues in correlation with increased CDX1 occupancy at PEAP. Also, we uncovered enrichment of CDX1 at PEAP in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing PCa cell lines, and increased CDX1 expression across PCa models overexpressing PVT1 exon 9. Targeting the predicted CDX1 binding motif within PEAP with a custom-designed antisense oligonucleotide disrupted CDX1 occupancy at PEAP, significantly inhibited expression of PVT1 exon 9, PCa cell proliferation and migration. Together, these results define a novel CDX1-PEAP signaling axis in which promoter methylation modulates CDX1 access to an internal regulatory element at PVT1, driving oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 overexpression. This work uncovers a novel regulatory mechanism in aggressive PCa and highlights the CDX1-PEAP axis as a potentially targetable node for therapeutic intervention in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing aggressive PCa.

title: DNA methylation-dependent CDX1 enrichment at PVT1 exon 9 associated promoter drives overexpression of PVT1 exon 9 in aggressive prostate cancer.

abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with its development and progression frequently driven by oncogenic alterations in EGFR and KRAS. Although molecularly targeted therapies, particularly Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs), have substantially improved clinical outcomes in selected patients, their long-term efficacy is frequently compromised by acquired resistance, tumor heterogeneity, and mutation-specific differences in therapeutic response. These limitations underscore the need for alternative strategies capable of selectively targeting oncogenic drivers while minimizing irreversible genomic alterations. RNA-targeted therapeutics have emerged as a potential therapeutic approach because they enable transient, programmable, and potentially reversible modulation of disease-associated transcripts without permanently modifying genomic DNA. Among these technologies, CRISPR-Cas13 and Adenosine Deaminase Acting on RNA (ADAR)-based editing systems offer distinct yet complementary mechanisms for manipulating oncogenic RNA. Cas13 enables sequence-specific recognition, degradation, or modulation of target transcripts, whereas engineered ADAR platforms facilitate site-directed Adenosine-to-Inosine (A-to-I) editing, allowing precise correction or functional recoding of selected RNA sequences. These approaches provide opportunities to selectively target clinically relevant mutant transcripts, including KRAS G12D/G12V and resistance-associated EGFR variants, while preserving their wild-type counterparts. Furthermore, Cas13-ADAR-based platforms may combine programmable RNA recognition with nucleotide-level editing to enhance specificity and expand the range of therapeutic applications. Emerging evidence from cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and animal models supports the feasibility of programmable RNA targeting; however, efficient tumor-specific delivery, off-target and collateral effects, immunogenicity, editing efficiency, and durability remain major barriers to clinical translation. Compared with permanent DNA editing, RNA editing offers potential advantages in reversibility, controllability, and reduced risk of persistent genomic off-target alterations. This review examines the molecular basis of EGFR- and KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma; recent advances in Cas13- and ADAR-mediated RNA targeting; delivery strategies; safety considerations; and preclinical progress, while highlighting the key challenges and future directions required to translate programmable RNA editing into precision therapies for lung adenocarcinoma.

title: Targeting Oncogenic EGFR and KRAS at the RNA Level: Emerging CRISPR-Cas13 and ADAR Strategies for Lung Adenocarcinoma.

abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, remains a major global public health challenge, particularly because of the emergence and spread of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains. Mutations in the katG gene, which encodes the catalase- peroxidase enzyme responsible for isoniazid activation, are among the major molecular mechanisms associated with isoniazid resistance in M. tuberculosis. CRISPR-Cas9 technology has emerged as a potential approach for targeting bacterial genetic determinants of antimicrobial resistance. However, its therapeutic application against intracellular M. tuberculosis remains challenging because effective delivery must overcome both host-cell and bacterial barriers. Exosomes, a subclass of extracellular vesicles, have attracted considerable attention as potential biological nanocarriers because of their biocompatibility and capacity to transport nucleic acids and proteins between cells. This review examines the molecular mechanisms underlying isoniazid resistance, recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 technology, the potential applications of exosome-based delivery systems, and the major challenges associated with their development for tuberculosis treatment. Unlike reviews that discuss CRISPR-based antimicrobial strategies and extracellular vesicle-mediated delivery separately, this review integrates these approaches to examine their potential application in targeting katG-associated isoniazid resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The review further evaluates the theoretical potential of extracellular vesicle-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 delivery for mutation- specific targeting of katG-associated isoniazid resistance, while considering the biological barriers that may limit its therapeutic application. Particular emphasis is placed on the need for mutation- specific correction rather than complete disruption of the katG gene, because loss of functional KatG activity can itself contribute to isoniazid resistance. However, the proposed exosomemediated CRISPR-Cas9 strategy has not yet been experimentally validated for targeting intracellular *M. tuberculosis*. Further in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo investigations are required to establish its delivery efficiency, mutation-specific editing feasibility, safety, and potential therapeutic effectiveness.

abstract: Skin cancer represents a major global public health burden, with melanoma accounting for the majority of skin cancer-related mortality despite the higher prevalence of non-melanoma skin cancers such as basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. Ultraviolet radiation, genetic susceptibility, and lifestyle-related factors drive disease initiation and progression, underscoring persistent challenges in early diagnosis and durable therapeutic control, particularly in advanced and treatment-resistant disease. Emerging evidence identifies non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs)-including microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs-as critical regulators of oncogenic signalling pathways involved in proliferation, angiogenesis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, immune evasion, and therapy resistance in skin cancer. Aberrant ncRNA expression patterns in tumor tissues and circulating biofluids are increasingly associated with disease stage, metastasis, and treatment response, highlighting their promise as diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive biomarkers. However, despite strong preclinical support, clinical translation of ncRNA-based therapeutics remains limited by challenges related to delivery efficiency, specificity, and safety. This review addresses a specific translational gap by integrating evidence on non-coding RNA (ncRNA) biology with nanoparticle-enabled delivery and CRISPR-based modulation in skin cancer. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing melanoma from non-melanoma skin cancers, evaluating ncRNAs according to their mechanistic and biomarker evidence, and critically assessing the preclinical and emerging clinical evidence for delivery and gene-modulation strategies. We further examine skin-specific delivery considerations, including topical and intratumoral administration, and discuss how nanoparticle platforms may facilitate localized delivery of ncRNA or CRISPR-associated cargos. Finally, we identify the major barriers to clinical translation, including biological heterogeneity, biomarker validation, delivery efficiency, off-target effects, immunogenicity, manufacturing complexity, and long-term safety, and propose an evidence-based framework for future precision oncology applications.

title: Nanoparticle and crispr strategies for non-coding RNA-based skin cancer therapy.

abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), a prevalent microvascular complication, remains a leading cause of irreversible vision loss globally. Traditional DR managements, including anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) intravitreal injections, are limited by high treatment burden, suboptimal patient adherence, and transient efficacy. In recent years, gene therapy has represented a promising alternative, enabling long-term, adjustable, and endogenous production of therapeutic agents through a single administration. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current understanding of DR from epidemiology, multimodal diagnosis, and molecular pathogenesis to the historical evolution and limitations of conventional therapies. Building upon these mechanistic insights, we further discuss recent advances in gene therapy for DR, extending beyond conventional anti-angiogenic strategies toward neurovascular unit protection, inflammation modulation, and metabolic regulation. Emerging gene-editing technologies, including Cas13-based RNA editing and prime editing (PE) for DNA correction, are also highlighted as promising next-generation therapeutic platforms. In addition, we summarized pioneering candidates in clinical trials, such as RGX-314, ADVM-022, and 4D-150, which have demonstrated promising efficacy in reducing the frequency of injections. Despite promising advances, we also discussed remaining challenges involving vector optimization, immune safety, transgene regulation, disease modeling, and patient stratification. Overall, gene therapy holds substantial potential to transform DR management from repetitive symptomatic intervention toward durable and personalized molecular treatment.
