abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelacarsen is an antisense oligonucleotide that reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). In a randomized placebo-controlled trial in patients with established cardiovascular disease, pelacarsen did not reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared to placebo. We further investigated the association of pelacarsen treatment with cardiovascular outcomes.
METHODS: We report the association of pelacarsen treatment with a primary composite end point of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization. Analyses included on-treatment, uninterrupted treatment, total primary end point events (first and recurrent events), landmark analyses classified by changes in and achieved lipoprotein(a) at 3 months, and key subgroups including baseline lipoprotein(a), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP), and time from qualifying event to enrollment.
RESULTS: For participants on treatment, a primary end point occurred in 434 participants (10.4%) randomly assigned to placebo and 380 participants (9.1%) assigned to pelacarsen (hazard ratio, 0.98; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.85 to 1.12). When evaluating participants with uninterrupted treatment, a primary end point event occurred in 167 participants (11.0%) in the pelacarsen group and 204 participants (10.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.89 to 1.34). When evaluating total primary end point events, there were 644 events in the pelacarsen group and 646 events in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.14). In landmark analyses evaluating participants alive and free of the composite end point at 3 months, when compared to placebo there was no association between pelacarsen treatment and the primary end point either in participants with reduction in lipoprotein(a) greater than or equal to the median (170 nmol/l) (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1.29) or in participants who achieved lipoprotein(a) lower than or equal to the median (69.5 nmol/l) (hazard ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.93 to 1.29). There was also no association between pelacarsen treatment and the primary end point in any of the evaluated key subgroups including classification by median baseline lipoprotein(a), LDL cholesterol, high-sensitivity CRP, or time from qualifying cardiovascular disease to enrollment.
CONCLUSIONS: Pelacarsen was not associated with a reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events when evaluated by treatment exposure, changes in or achieved lipoprotein(a) levels at 3 months, considering total events, or within subgroups of baseline lipoprotein(a), LDL cholesterol, or high-sensitivity CRP levels.

abstract: Great strides have been achieved in lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mediated mRNA delivery. However, traditional LNPs can induce undesirable side effects such as inflammatory reactions. Oxidative stress damage arising from ionizable lipids within LNPs is regarded as a major underlying cause of these adverse effects. Herein, we propose incorporating endogenous vitamin E (VE) into the tail moiety of commercial ionizable lipids to improve biosafety. Proof-of-concept investigations using SM-102-derived W3 confirm that this endogenous antioxidant modification substantially mitigates the inflammatory toxicity of mRNA-loaded LNPs. Following intravenous administration, W3 LNPs markedly decrease the levels of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, demonstrating an improved safety profile compared to SM-102 LNPs. Further analysis reveals that W3 LNPs significantly reduce intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, alleviate oxidative stress damage, thereby inhibiting the activation of key inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB. Of note, the optimized formulation, sW3 LNPs enable efficient mRNA delivery to the spleen, with stronger antitumor efficacy and higher safety than SM-102 LNPs. In summary, W3 lipid confers minimal inflammatory adverse effects while preserving excellent delivery capability, which indicates that the VE-engineered LNPs possess great potential to serve as powerful and multifunctional platforms for next-generation mRNA therapeutics.

title: Vitamin E-Engineered Anti-Inflammatory Lipid Nanoparticles for Safer mRNA Delivery.

abstract:
CAD is driven by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and is a major cause of myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death. Despite contemporary secondary prevention including lipid lowering, revascularization when indicated, and antiplatelet therapy, participants with established CAD, particularly those post-ACS, remain at clinically meaningful residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events.

Intensifying antithrombotic therapy can reduce ischemic events but typically increases bleeding, as exemplified by the addition of low dose rivaroxaban to aspirin in stable atherosclerotic disease. This persistent efficacy-safety trade-off supports development of antithrombotic approaches that reduce pathological thrombosis while preserving hemostasis.

RBD1119 is a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that targets factor XI mRNA in hepatocytes. The GalNAc moiety binds the asialoglycoprotein receptor on hepatocyte surfaces, enabling receptor mediated endocytosis and preferential hepatic uptake. Once internalized, RBD1119 mediates cleavage of factor XI mRNA via the RNA interference pathway, reducing hepatic factor XI expression and lowering circulating factor XI levels.

This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase II trial will evaluate the PD, safety, and PK of subcutaneously administered RBD1119 in participants with stable coronary artery disease (CAD).

description:
CAD is caused by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and remains a leading cause of MI, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death, with substantial residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events even after standard secondary prevention. More intensive antithrombotic therapy can lower ischemic events, but this benefit is often offset by increased bleeding, highlighting the need for treatments that better separate antithrombotic efficacy from bleeding risk. Factor XI, part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, has emerged as a promising target because its inhibition reduces thrombin amplification and prolongs aPTT without affecting prothrombin time, suggesting potential for safer anticoagulation with less disruption of normal hemostasis.

The trial comprises screening, treatment, and long-term safety follow-up periods. Participants will be allocated to one of three different dose levels of RBD1119 or placebo: low-dose (n=40), medium-dose (n=60), high-dose (n=60) or placebo (n=40). Approximately 200 participants will be randomized.

Randomization to the RBD1119 low-dose dose group and corresponding placebo proceeds without dose-specific staggering. Randomization to the medium-dose group is initially limited to 10 participants, comprising 8 participants assigned to RBD1119 medium-dose and 2 assigned to placebo. Further randomization is paused until participants have received Dose X on Day Y and completed safety follow-up through Day 43. Randomization resumes only after IDMC review, a recommendation to continue, and Sponsor authorization. Initiation of the high-dose group requires prior IDMC review of the initial medium-dose cohort and Sponsor authorization. The same initial cohort, safety follow-up, IDMC review, and authorization process is then applied to the high-dose group. A planned IDMC review will not be delayed solely because fewer than all 10 participants in an initial dose cohort have received the second dose or completed follow-up through Day 43.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are a treatment modality for genetic diseases, binding to ribonucleic acid (RNA) with high specificity, with downstream effects that eventually reduce, restore, or modify protein expression through distinct mechanisms. Conjugating ASOs to targeting ligands has emerged as a promising strategy to improve tissue-specific delivery, but there remains a lack of binding assays to study this class of therapeutic conjugates. Here, we develop streamlined assays that assess the binding kinetics of both the ASO and the targeting ligand using biolayer interferometry (BLI). The BLI biosensor facilitates immobilization of a biotinylated oligonucleotide, which can then hybridize an ASO conjugate and subsequently measure its binding affinity to the ligand target (e.g., antibody or receptor) through analysis of a BLI sensorgram. The utility of this biomolecular sandwich binding assay is demonstrated with phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomers (PMOs) and peptide nucleic acids (PNAs) conjugated to a peptide or protein ligand. We show that this assay can be used to detect cellular binding and predict in vitro efficacy. The methods developed here can be leveraged to accelerate the development of next-generation ASO therapeutics.

title: A Biomolecular Sandwich Assay to Characterize the Binding Properties of Antisense Oligonucleotide Conjugates.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hemoglobinopathies are associated with lifelong multimorbidity. In addition to optimized supportive care, disease-modifying and potentially (functionally) curative therapies are available.
OBJECTIVE: To review modern treatment options for thalassemias and sickle cell disease in adults.
RESULTS: In beta-thalassemia, luspatercept targets ineffective erythropoiesis, while mitapivat, an oral pyruvate kinase activator, improves erythrocyte energy metabolism. Both therapies improve anemia and may reduce transfusion burden but are not curative. Through clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9)-mediated gene editing, exagamglogene autotemcel reactivates fetal hemoglobin production, enabling transfusion independence in beta-thalassemia and preventing recurrent severe vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease. Hydroxyurea remains the cornerstone of pharmacological therapy for sickle cell disease. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and gene editing offer the possibility of a (functional) cure but require careful assessment of organ function, fertility, and treatment-related risks.
CONCLUSION: Key advances include the optimization of established supportive therapies and the establishment of specialized centers providing access to potentially (functionally) curative treatments. In adults, the anticipated benefits, pre-existing irreversible organ damage, conditioning-related risks, potential long-term complications, and access to treatment must be carefully considered at an early stage.

title: [Modern treatments for hemoglobinopathies in adults].

abstract: Overexpression of leucine-rich repeat-containing protein 15 (LRRC15) is closely linked to cancer progression and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), making it a promising therapeutic target. Conventional single-target approaches suffer from limited efficacy and off-target effects. Here, we develop a dual-targeting nanoplatform based on Ag2S@ZIF-8 nanoparticles (NPs) and modified with hyaluronic acid (HA) for imaging-guided photothermal-gene editing synergistic therapy against LRRC15-related diseases. The resulting Ag2S-crRNA/Cas12a@ZIF-8@HA (ACZH) NPs deliver CRISPR RNA (crRNA) for sequence-specific LRRC15 recognition, together with HSP70 promoter-driven Cas12a plasmids. Ag2S NPs enable real-time NIR-II fluorescence imaging and generate localized hyperthermia (>42°C) that activates the HSP70 promoter to induce Cas12a expression and subsequent LRRC15 editing. In breast and lung cancer xenograft models, ACZH NPs achieve tumor inhibition rates of 81.37% and 82.5%, respectively; in an RA model, they reduce joint inflammation, prevent cartilage erosion, and promote bone repair. These findings offer a safe and effective strategy for LRRC15-related diseases.

abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing expands transcriptomic diversity, yet its contribution to organismal aging remains unclear. Here, we show that ADAR enzyme ADR-2 is specifically required for lifespan extension under metabolic stress. Loss of adr-2 abolished the longevity of mitochondrial dysfunction (isp-1) and dietary restriction (eat-2) mutants, while leaving lifespan extension mediated by reduced insulin/IGF-1 (daf-2) or mTOR (rsks-1) signaling intact. RNA editome analysis revealed increased ADR-2-dependent editing of three paralogous transmembrane genes, trel-1, trel-2, and trel-3, in long-lived isp-1 and eat-2 animals. Deletion of these genes partially restored lifespan in adr-2-deficient mutants, establishing a genetic interaction between adr-2 and trel genes. TREL proteins localize to lysosome-related organelles, and loss of trel genes alters the intracellular distribution of a fluorescent heme analog. Consistent with this, the human TREL homolog MFSD7 (SLC49A3) displays similar lysosomal localization and influences heme analog compartmentalization. Together, these findings uncover a context-dependent role for ADR-2 in longevity and implicate TREL proteins as a regulatory node linking metabolic stress to intracellular heme homeostasis and lifespan regulation.

title: RNA deaminase modulates metabolic stress-induced longevity in Caenorhabditis elegans.

abstract: Chikungunya fever (CHIKF) is an acute mosquito-borne disease caused by chikungunya virus (CHIKV). Driven by globalization, climate change and expanding vector habitats, its geographic range continues to widen; in 2025 it produced the largest outbreak ever recorded in China, with more than 25,800 locally transmitted cases across all 21 prefecture-level cities of Guangdong. Beyond acute fever, rash and arthralgia, a substantial proportion of patients develop chronic arthritis, which accounts for much of the disease burden. This review summarizes the etiological features, life cycle, epidemiology and ongoing evolution of CHIKV, and critically evaluates progress in antiviral drugs and vaccines, together with vector control, microbiome-based approaches and One Health governance. No specific antiviral has yet been approved: compounds targeting viral entry, RNA capping, protease activity and genome replication inhibit CHIKV selectively in cell culture but remain at preclinical or early clinical stages, and host-directed agents are further constrained by host toxicity. Two vaccines are now licensed-the live-attenuated vaccine Ixchiq, whose use has been progressively restricted following post-marketing safety signals, and the virus-like particle vaccine Vimkunya-while inactivated, chimeric, viral-vectored and mRNA candidates remain earlier in development. For all countermeasures, whether the envelope substitutions carried by recently emerged strains, including E2-L210Q and E2-I211 T within the immunodominant domain B, will erode protection remains experimentally unresolved. Collectively, CHIKV control still faces the absence of approved antivirals, incompletely defined long-term vaccine safety and breadth, and ongoing vector population expansion. Future work should prioritize broad-spectrum antivirals and next-generation vaccines, promote multidisciplinary collaboration, and strengthen integrated governance under the One Health framework.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07555392..Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06669208..

abstract: The primary purpose of the study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of CMP-002 in participants with SYNGAP1-related disorder.
description: ASCEND is a global, Phase 1/2, multicenter, randomized, double-blind (Sponsor-open), controlled, multiple-ascending dose (MAD) study to assess the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics, of CMP-002 in participants with SYNGAP1-related disorder (SRD). The study consists of a Baseline Period in which participants will undergo screening assessments to establish the baseline for clinical study assessments. The Baseline Period is followed by a Treatment Period consisting of 3 planned dose level cohorts wherein each participant will receive 3 doses of CMP-002 administered intrathecally (IT) or a control procedure on Days 1, 29, and 85. Each dose level cohort includes a minimum of 8 participants randomized in a 3:1 ratio (CMP-002: control). Following the completion of Dose 3, participants will be followed for an additional 24 weeks in the Follow-up Period.

abstract: Guanidine-bridged nucleic acid (GuNA) is a bridged nucleic acid analog with high binding affinity toward complementary strands along with high nuclease resistance. GuNA has been developed to improve pharmacokinetics and safety profiles of phosphorothioate modified gapmers. Here, we evaluated antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) modified with combination of GuNA and 2'-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) and found that the dual-modification strategy could significantly improve knockdown activity in vitro and in vivo. Long-term efficacy evaluation showed that intracerebroventricularly administered GuNA-modified gapmers stayed active for over 24 weeks in mouse brain. Furthermore, we observed that GuNA-modified gapmers could evade lymphocyte-derived immune responses and kept ASO-induced toxicity in check. Taken together, the results of this study demonstrate that GuNA modification can improve the functional potential of ASOs, especially in the central nervous system.

abstract: Neural repair research increasingly combines molecular interventions with engineered environments that support axonal growth and circuit function. This narrative review examines neuronal growth pathways, direct cellular reprogramming, conductive scaffolds, extracellular-vesicle delivery, and neuroimmune and neurovascular interactions. Genetic studies of PTEN/mTOR, SOCS3/STAT3, and growth-associated transcription factors provide a biological foundation for investigating targeted gene regulation. CRISPR-based editing and transcriptional control offer distinct tools for exploring these pathways. Conductive and stimulus-responsive materials provide experimental interfaces for structural guidance, electrical stimulation, and local molecular delivery. Their integration with gene-regulatory systems is presented as a conceptual strategy for coordinating molecular and biophysical interventions. Organoids, single-cell and spatial profiling, and electrophysiological measurements offer complementary approaches to characterizing cell identity and network responses. Clinical studies targeting axon-growth inhibition provide a separate translational evidence stream, with outcomes interpreted according to intervention, injury characteristics, and trial design. Priorities for integrated repair systems include cell-specific delivery, material stability, durable circuit function, and longitudinal safety assessment. A prospective digital-twin workflow is proposed to connect biological measurements with computational predictions and experimentally evaluated intervention choices. Together, these research directions support a framework for studying programmable neural repair across molecular, cellular, and systems levels.

abstract: Gene delivery is now a clinically established modality, but one of its central translational challenges remains: therapeutic performance emerges from a cascade of biological processes rather than from a single step. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, and oligonucleotide conjugates undergo biological transformation, distribution and tissue access, cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, endosomal escape, and ultimately functional payload delivery. The contribution of each process to the therapeutic outcome is context dependent and may shift with formulation, route of administration, target tissue, payload, and disease state. Consequently, transfection efficiency remains a necessary and widely used endpoint, but as a single aggregate readout it cannot by itself indicate which upstream process, biodistribution, uptake, trafficking, or endosomal escape, is rate-limiting for a given formulation, route, or tissue; resolving that bottleneck is the measurable attribute an in vitro-in vivo relationship must be built around. Classical in vitro-in vivo correlation (IVIVC) concepts were developed for simpler relationships, but their underlying principle remains relevant: identifying a measurable product attribute or process that governs in vivo performance. As pharmaceutical systems have become more complex, biopredictive methodologies have logically progressed toward process-resolved assays, systems-level understanding, and mechanistic modeling. Applying this principle to non-viral gene delivery does not imply that a validated IVIVC, or a regulatory biowaiver built on one, yet exists for these systems; rather, it asks whether the same underlying logic, identifying which step in a multi-step cascade is rate limiting and can be represented by a measurable in vitro assay, can be meaningfully extended from simpler dosage forms to a biologically complex delivery process. This review proposes a pathway toward IVIVC for non-viral gene delivery as a delivery cascade comprising three interconnected layers: (i) the Nanoparticle Biodistribution Layer, spanning circulation, biological transformation, and tissue access; (ii) the Cellular Delivery Dynamics Layer, encompassing cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal escape; and (iii) the Functional Therapeutic Action Layer, linking productive delivery to pharmacodynamic response. Each layer is matched with assays that isolate individual processes and expose where formulation performance becomes limiting. These layers have traditionally been studied by largely separate scientific communities, making their integration essential for understanding how performance gains or losses propagate through the delivery cascade. Rather than proposing a holistic IVIVC that does not yet exist for non-viral gene delivery, this framework provides a mechanistic roadmap for building it, moving formulation development from empirical screening toward stepwise biopredictive evidence and, ultimately, IVIVC for complex gene delivery systems.

abstract: This phase III trial tests how well the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy works for treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma. Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to a molecule called GD2, which is found on the surface of neuroblastoma cells, but is not present on many healthy or normal cells in the body. When dinutuximab binds to the neuroblastoma cells, it helps signal the immune system to kill the tumor cells. This helps the cells of the immune system kill the cancer cells, this is a type of immunotherapy. When chemotherapy and immunotherapy are given together, during the same treatment cycle, it is called chemoimmunotherapy. This clinical trial randomly assigns patients to receive either standard chemotherapy and surgery or chemoimmunotherapy (chemotherapy plus dinutuximab) and surgery during Induction therapy. Chemotherapy drugs administered during Induction include, cyclophosphamide, topotecan, cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin. These drugs work in different ways to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing or by stopping them from spreading. Upon completion of 5 cycles of Induction therapy, a disease evaluation is completed to determine how well the treatment worked. If the tumor responds to therapy, patients receive a tandem transplantation with stem cell rescue. If the tumor has little improvement or worsens, patients receive chemoimmunotherapy on Extended Induction. During Extended Induction, dinutuximab is given with irinotecan, temozolomide. Patients with a good response to therapy move on to Consolidation therapy, when very high doses of chemotherapy are given at two separate points to kill any remaining cancer cells. Following, transplant, radiation therapy is given to the site where the cancer originated (primary site) and to any other areas that are still active at the end of Induction. The final stage of therapy is Post-Consolidation. During Post-Consolidation, dinutuximab is given with isotretinoin, with the goal of maintaining the response achieved with the previous therapy. Adding dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy may be better at treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if the event-free survival (EFS) of patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma assigned to early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction differs from that of patients who are not assigned to treatment that includes early chemoimmunotherapy.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine if early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction therapy improves end of Induction (EOI) response rates and overall survival (OS) for patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.

II. To determine response rates, EFS, and OS following an Extended Induction regimen with chemoimmunotherapy in patients with progressive disease or a poor response to Induction therapy.

III. To compare the toxicities experienced by patients treated with chemoimmunotherapy during Induction versus those experienced by patients treated with standard Induction and to describe toxicities experienced during Extended Induction.

IV. To determine GD2 expression on tumor tissue and tumor cells in bone marrow and assess for associations with response and outcome.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. To describe the association between tumor and host factors and outcomes in patients receiving protocol therapy.

II. To evaluate circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease at baseline and during therapy, and assess for associations with response and outcome.

III. To compare patterns of failure between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during induction.

IV. To determine the effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms on end of Induction response rates, EFS, and OS.

V. To explore the impact of high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL) and its therapy, including the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy, on functional and quality of life outcomes in patients with HRNBL, as measured by caregiver (parent/legal guardian) and patient questionnaires.

VI. To describe the adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens, including those obtained by percutaneous core needle biopsy.

VII. To explore the associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology.

VIII. To develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response based on diagnostic MIBG scans. (Imaging Objective) IX. To compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and poor end of induction response (PEIR) and good end of induction response (GEIR) determination. (Imaging Objective) X. To describe late toxicities (including impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and incidence of secondary malignancy) in patients treated with dinutuximab during Induction or Extended Induction to late toxicities in patients who have not received dinutuximab during these phases of therapy.

XI. To evaluate whether reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts.

XII. To compare post-transplant complications between treatment arms, and assess for associations with outcome.

XIII. To assess for associations between EOI response (including good end of Induction response \[GEIR\] and poor end of Induction response \[PEIR\]) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).

XIV. To describe and compare the changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRFs) between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during Induction and associate with surgical outcomes and local failure rates following primary tumor resection.

XV. To bank serial samples of blood, bone marrow, and tumor tissue for future research.

OUTLINE: Patients receive Induction cycle 1 and are then randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

INDUCTION CYCLE 1: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity.

ARM A:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients then receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide orally (PO), via nasogastric tube (NG), or via gastric tube (G-tube) on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantations (HSCTs) during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion, patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2. Patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO twice daily (BID) on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, echocardiogram (ECHO) or multigated acquisition scan (MUGA), bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), iodine-123 meta-iodobenzylguanidine (I-MIBG) scan and possible fluorodeoxyglucose position emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan throughout the study.

ARM B:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes, topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide PO, via NG tube, or via G-tube on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous HSCTs during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2, patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO BID on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, ECHO or MUGA, bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, CT scan, MRI, I-MIBG scan and possible FDG-PET scan throughout the study.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 3, 6, 9,12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, and 60 months and then periodically for up to 10 years from enrollment.

outcomes.description: EFS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B to first episode of disease relapse or progression, second malignancy, or death, or until last contact if no event has occurred.
outcomes.measure: Event free survival (EFS)

outcomes.description: The response rate will be calculated among all evaluable patients at end of Induction. Responders are defined as patients who achieve a \>= partial response per the revised 2017 International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria (INRC)
outcomes.measure: End of Induction (EOI) response rate
outcomes.time_frame: From randomization to end of extended Induction, up to 12 months

outcomes.description: OS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B until death, or until last contact if patient is alive.
outcomes.measure: Overall survival (OS)

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients with at least one grade 3 or higher non-hematologic toxicity or grade 4 or higher hematologic toxicity during protocol therapy, graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0, will be reported.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of adverse events

outcomes.description: Dinutuximab binding to pre-therapy patient tumor samples will be measured and categorized as high or low.
outcomes.measure: GD2 expression

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in Arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between tumor and host factors (including tumor ALK and other somatic mutations, copy-number aberrations, gene fusions, gene expression, and pathogenic germline variants) and chemo-immunotherapy during Induction with outcome.
outcomes.measure: Association between tumor and host factors and outcomes

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by comparing the proportion of patients with detectable vs. non-detectable tumor markers (including circulating tumor deoxyribonucleic acid, circulating free DNA, circulating tumor cells, and immune function profiling) between Arms A and B during and after induction and post-consolidation therapy using chi-squared tests at each individual time point, and Cochran's Q across time points to determine if there is a consistent difference in proportions between arms across time. In addition, the tumor markers will be analyzed as continuous variables using longitudinal data analysis methodology such as mixed effects models or generalized estimating equations as appropriate.
outcomes.measure: Circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease

outcomes.description: The impact of early or late chemoimmunotherapy during Induction on the probability of the involvement of a specific disease site at first relapse will be evaluated using Fisher's exact test.
outcomes.measure: Patterns of failure

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between telomere maintenance mechanism and chemoimmunotherapy during Induction with outcome. Patients will be classified into 3 groups by telomere maintenance mechanism (TMM) based on messenger ribonucleic acid expression of TERT and analysis of telomeric DNA C-circles: telomerase (TERT) positive, alternative of lengthening of telomeres (ALT) positive, or no identified TMM.
outcomes.measure: Effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms

outcomes.description: Will descriptively summarize and compare the total Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale scores, total sub-domain scores, and individual symptom scores between patients randomized to receive dinutuximab during Induction (Arm B) to those of patients randomized to standard Induction (Arm A).
outcomes.measure: Functional and quality of life outcomes
outcomes.time_frame: At serial time points during Induction, Extended Induction, Post-Consolidation, and at the end of therapy

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by descriptively comparing the successful delineation of histologic classification, MYCN amplification status, and ALK status via the traditional method of obtaining tissue for diagnosis, open surgical biopsy, versus the less invasive percutaneous core needle biopsy.
outcomes.measure: Adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens

outcomes.description: Kaplan-Meier curves of EFS and OS will be generated and used to calculate 3-year EFS and OS estimates. Associations between social determinants of health (SDOH) and survival outcomes and time to receipt of dinutuximab will be evaluated with univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard models. Log-binomial regression will be used to estimate risk ratios and 95% CI for the occurrence of dinutuximab consent to randomization and therapy receipt by SDOH exposure. Effect modification of outcomes as a function of poverty, stratified by race/ethnicity, will be explored.
outcomes.measure: Associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology

outcomes.description: Scans will be given as input to a convolutional neural network trained to predict EOI response.
outcomes.measure: Develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response (imaging objective)
outcomes.time_frame: At diagnosis, EOI, during Extended Induction, and end of Extended Induction

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by calculating the percentage of patients receiving the same EOI institutional and centrally reviewed determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and PEIR and GEIR. In addition, Cohen's kappa will be calculated to evaluate the concordance in each of these response measures.
outcomes.measure: Compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components, and PEIR and GEIR determination (imaging objective)

outcomes.description: Will be addressed by calculating the proportion of treated patients with each late effect, including but not limited to impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and secondary malignancy. A 95% confidence interval will be placed on each proportion.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of late toxicities

outcomes.description: The cumulative incidence of local progression (CILP) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI and GEIR on this study will be compared to the CILP rate of 11.2±1.8% observed on ANBL0532 using Gray's test.
outcomes.measure: Reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by calculating the incidence of endothelial injury complications and non-relapse mortality within 100 days of transplant, transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA), severe TA-TMA, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) on Arms A and B and comparing between arms with a chi-squared test. The impact of TA-TMA occurrence on the timing or exclusion of subsequent therapy and interventions utilized to treat the TA-TMA, and associations with outcomes (EFS and OS) will be assessed.
outcomes.measure: Post-transplant complications

outcomes.description: Log-rank tests will be used to explore the association between EOI response (using both the revised INRC and GEIR/PEIR classification) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).
outcomes.measure: Associations between end of induction (EOI) response and individual response components

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients in the analytic cohort for whom each particular IDRF and also the presence of any IDRF is absent prior to surgical resection will be computed. McNemar's test for paired observations will be applied to determine whether there is a difference in the proportion of each IDRF and any IDRF present before and after initial therapy, and conditional logistic regression will be used to compare between treatment arms A and B. The IDRF status after initial therapy and whether there has been a change from diagnosis will be associated with surgical outcome (complete vs. incomplete resection, presence or absence of surgical complications) using chi-squared tests, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test. The association of IDRF status with presence or absence of local failure after primary tumor resection will also be evaluated using a chi-squared test, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel.
outcomes.measure: Changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRF)

abstract: Since its discovery, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) has revolutionized biomedical science and engineering with its ability to recognize and edit gene sequences with high specificity and precision. Despite the growing interest in using these capabilities to address environmental and sustainability challenges, the broader potential of CRISPR in environmental systems remains unexplored relative to its biomedical applications. Here, we provide a critical perspective on the emerging use of CRISPR for pollution management, ecological conservation, and environmental monitoring. Rather than viewing CRISPR solely as a gene-editing or biosensing technology, we consider both capabilities together to examine how advances in CRISPR engineering can translate into practical environmental solutions. We highlight the fundamental principles behind CRISPR-based editing and sensing and evaluate the challenges that constrain their transition from proof-of-concept experiments to field deployment, including off-target effects, delivery methods, ecological risks, and low sensitivity. Addressing these hurdles requires a multifaceted approach that integrates emerging technologies such as reversible CRISPR technology, amplification and cascade reactions, and machine learning, with strict regulatory oversight and rigorous risk assessments. This perspective identifies critical strengths, weaknesses, and research priorities for advancing CRISPR from laboratory technology toward robust tools for environmental applications.

abstract:
This is a randomised, actively controlled Phase IIb trial to evaluate the safety and pharmacodynamics (PD) of two blinded doses of subcutaneously administered vortosiran and open-label apixaban in patients with AF.

The trial consists of three groups including 50 participants each. The participants will be randomized to either the low dose group or the high dose group receiving vortosiran or to the group receiving apixaban. The treatment will be open-label for vortosiran vs apixaban. The vortosiran dose will be blinded to patients and investigators.

Both the low- and the high-dose group will receive two doses of vortosiran, the first dose at Day X and the second at Day Y. After 24 weeks, at the end of the vortosiran treatment period, the participants will start an open-label part of the trial and will be switched to standard-of-care apixaban treatment until Week 64 (End of Trial; EOT). Participants in the open-label apixaban arm will receive apixaban as standard of care during the entire trial.

description:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is among the most prevalent cardiovascular conditions, affecting approximately 2 4% of the adult population worldwide. AF represents the most common sustained supraventricular arrhythmia and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and health-care burden. Patients with AF are at an elevated risk of thromboembolic complications, particularly ischemic stroke and systemic embolism, while also facing an increased risk of bleeding associated with long-term antithrombotic therapy administered to prevent these complications. The principal aim of management in AF is to prevent stroke while minimizing haemorrhagic risk through careful risk stratification for both thromboembolic risk and bleeding risk, and informed and individualised treatment selections.

According to current guideline recommendations, oral anticoagulation is recommended for stroke prevention and may be guided by CHA2DS2 -VASc clinical risk assessment tool. Nonvitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs, also referred to as direct oral anticoagulants, or DOACs) are preferred over vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) in most cases due to their superior safety profile and lower incidence of intracranial bleeding. Bleeding risk can be assessed using validated tools such as HAS-BLED, and modifiable risk factors should be addressed to reduce overall treatment-related complications.

Despite a superior efficacy-safety profile of NOACs relative to VKAs, patients treated with NOACs remain at residual risk for stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular mortality. Furthermore, although NOACs are associated with reduced rates of intracranial haemorrhage compared with VKAs, they still confer a considerable risk of major bleeding and clinically relevant non-major bleeding events. Consequently, the clinical need for strategies that further optimize the balance between thromboembolic prevention and bleeding risk in patients with AF remains.

Recent advances have positioned coagulation factor XI (FXI) inhibition as a promising strategy in anti-thrombotic drug development. FXI is a crucial element of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, and genetic FXI deficiency (haemophilia C) is typically associated with only mild bleeding even in complete deficiency, suggesting the potential for improved safety compared to conventional anti-thrombotic drugs by disengaging physiologic haemostasis from pathologic, intraluminal thrombosis. FXI inhibition reliably prolongs activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) in vitro, and epidemiological studies demonstrate that inherited FXI deficiency confers protection against venous thromboembolism (VTE) and ischemic stroke. Conversely, elevated circulating activated FXI (FXIa) is linked to higher risks of ischemic stroke, VTE, and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Contemporary research utilizing coagulometric assays has confirmed FXIa and tissue factor activation in patients with stable coronary artery disease, ACS of less than 12 hours' duration, and heart failure, reinforcing FXI's role as a pathogenic factor in these conditions.

From the patient perspective, the limitations of current DOAC-based strategies extend beyond rare catastrophic haemorrhage to include a spectrum of patient-relevant bleeding and treatment burdens that erode quality of life and adherence. Easy bruising, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, and minor gastrointestinal bleeding are often labelled nuisance or non-major events in clinical trials, but patients describe these as anxiety-provoking, stigmatizing, and disruptive to daily activities. Such events, together with polypharmacy, twice-daily dosing for some agents, drug drug interactions, and the need for uninterrupted long-term therapy, frequently lead to missed doses, dose reductions, or unsupervised discontinuation of DOACs, which in turn compromises stroke protection at the population level. In parallel, important patient subgroups including those with advanced chronic kidney disease or dialysis, advanced liver disease, prior intracranial haemorrhage, or frailty have been underrepresented in pivotal DOAC trials and often withheld treatment or remain untreated because of bleeding concerns. By targeting FXI, vortosiran has the potential to dissociate pathological thrombosis from physiological haemostasis, and to deliver sustained antithrombotic protection with a lower risk bleeding than currently available therapies and an adherence profile that is better aligned with patients' priorities and lived experience.

Clinical trials targeting FXI inhibition in the context of cardiovascular disease, including AF, are ongoing or recently completed. Several Phase 2 and 3 trials are investigating FXI/FXIa inhibitors by use of different modalities such as monoclonal antibodies and small molecules across multiple high-risk groups, evaluating efficacy and bleeding outcomes against standard anticoagulants for stroke prevention in AF (SPAF). These studies collectively support the notion that FXI/FXIa may be a favourable anticoagulation target, capable of reducing thrombotic events with a lower side effect profile, especially bleeding, compared to traditional agents. However, while several trials confirm safety advantages, data on efficacy remain to be further demonstrated, necessitating continued research focus. Vortosiran is an N-acetyl galactosamine (GalNAc) conjugated small interfering ribonucleic acid (siRNA), enabling highly specific and highly durable enrichment of the siRNA in hepatocytes, offering a modality specifically inhibiting the production of FXI. Vortosiran is under development to achieve a durable antithrombotic effect by reducing the levels of FXI.

The rationale for the current trial is based on data from multiple Phase 2 and 3 studies of FXI/FXIa inhibitors that have assessed FXI clotting activity and the effect on venous thrombosis inhibition, and is currently being tested for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation patients. Based on the collective observations for these studies, that FXI clotting activity inhibition translates into a lower risk of thrombosis with a lower risk of bleeding compared to standard of care, the ongoing Phase 3 studies, and that vortosiran treatment can achieve identical or even higher degrees of FXI clotting activity inhibition, there is a rationale that vortosiran could potentially improve benefit-risk balance for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation compared to standard of care with FXa inhibitors.

abstract:
This is a prospective, multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation Phase I study using a Bayesian Optimal Interval (BOIN) design. The study will evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of circular RNA-HM2002 injection administered as a single transendocardial myocardial injection in patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) who are refractory to optimal medical therapy and unsuitable for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

Three dose levels (5 mg, 15 mg, and 30 mg) are planned, with 3 participants per dose level and a total planned enrollment of at least 9 participants. The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or the recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D).

Dose escalation decisions will be made by a Safety Review Committee (SRC) according to predefined BOIN rules with a target toxicity probability of 25%. Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) will be assessed during the 28-day observation period after administration. All participants will be followed for 6 months after administration for safety and preliminary efficacy assessments.

outcomes.description:
The assessment covers 5 domains-physical limitation, anginal stability, anginal frequency, treatment satisfaction, and disease perception-to comprehensively evaluate the patient's angina-related health status during the past 4 weeks.

For each item, the 5 response options are scored with ordinal values starting at 1, where 1 corresponds to the response representing the lowest level of functioning. Item scores are summed within each of the 5 dimensions. Raw scores for each dimension are then transformed to a standard score: standard score = (observed score - minimum possible score for the dimension) × 100 / (maximum possible score - minimum possible score). The maximum score for each dimension is 100. Each dimension will be analyzed separately, and no composite score across the 5 dimensions will be calculated.
outcomes.measure: Seattle Angina Questionnaire (SAQ)
outcomes.time_frame: Change from baseline at Day 28,Month 3 and Month 6 post-procedure

outcomes.description:
Changes in participants' generic health-related quality of life will be assessed. The EuroQol 5-Dimension 5-Level questionnaire (EQ-5D-5L, Appendix 7) is among the most widely used preference-based health utility measures internationally and comprises two parts:

EQ-5D-5L descriptive system: comprising 5 dimensions-mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression-each graded on 5 levels of severity, from "no problems" to "unable to / extreme problems." EQ visual analogue scale (EQ VAS): recording the participant's self-rated overall health status on the day of assessment on a vertical scale from 0 ("worst imaginable health state") to 100 ("best imaginable health state").

In the descriptive system, the level selected for each dimension corresponds to a score, and the combination of the 5 responses can be converted into a health utility index using an appropriate value set. For the EQ VAS, higher scores represent better self-perceived overall health statu.
outcomes.measure: EQ-5D-5L questionnaire
outcomes.time_frame: Change from baseline at Day 28,Month 3 and Month 6 post-procedure

abstract: Extracellular vesicles encode a universal language of intercellular communication-the 'ommunicome'-yet clinical translation has been constrained by extreme EV heterogeneity and the inability to trace circulating mRNA to its cellular origin. This review synthesizes three paradigm-shifting innovations that overcome these barriers: (1) the SCOPE platform, a CRISPR-Cas13/hybridization chain reaction system achieving single-molecule sensitivity at single-vesicle resolution; (2) computational spatial deconvolution enabling non-invasive, cell-type-resolved phenotyping of inaccessible tissues from standard biofluid samples and (3) the Functional Communication Circuits (FCC) framework-a network-based paradigm proposing that EV diagnostic power resides in correlated network relationships rather than isolated biomarkers. We critically evaluate SCOPE against competing technologies, establish its unique diagnostic niche and present clinical validation across oncology, neurology and cardiology. The FCC framework resolves the stoichiometric paradox of EV biology by demonstrating that low per-vesicle cargo copy numbers aggregate across the circulating EV pool to generate statistically robust population-level correlation signals. A translational roadmap encompasses pre-analytical standardization (including MISEV guidelines), targeted immunoaffinity enrichment and clinically actionable EV Communication Scores that distil multi-omics complexity into interpretable metrics. Five unresolved challenges, including the L1CAM controversy in neural EV isolation, SCOPE multiplexing limits and the absence of prospective FCC validation cohorts, are identified with concrete experimental solutions. The convergence of single-vesicle analysis, spatial deconvolution and functional circuit modelling is hypothesized to transform liquid biopsy from passive detection into active, systems-level interrogation of human disease.

abstract: CDK12/13 regulate transcription through phosphorylation of Serine 2 (S2) in the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II and have emerged as potential therapeutic targets in cancer. Here, we report the development of CTX-439, an orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive small-molecule inhibitor of CDK12/13. CTX-439 inhibits S2 phosphorylation and downregulates genes involved in DNA damage repair, resulting in antitumor activity in vitro and in vivo, including in breast cancer patient-derived xenograft models. A CRISPR activation screen identified the anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members BCL-2 and BCL-xL as mediators of resistance to CTX-439. Accordingly, combined inhibition of CDK12/13 and BCL-2/BCL-xL induced apoptosis and enhanced tumor growth suppression in xenograft models. Mechanistically, CTX-439 reduces MCL1 protein levels through transcriptional readthrough, shifting cell survival dependency toward BCL-2 and BCL-xL. Together, these findings identify a vulnerability induced by CDK12/13 inhibition and provide a rationale for combining CTX-439 with BCL-2/BCL-xL inhibitors.

abstract: Advances in gene delivery technologies have opened new avenues for modulating platelet function and expanding their applications in cell-based therapies. However, as anucleate cells, platelets have long faced the dual challenge of low transfection efficiency and susceptibility to activation during genetic manipulation. Here, we report a rationally optimized lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation for efficient and low-activation mRNA delivery to platelets by systematically tuning the 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC)/cholesterol molar ratio. Five LNP formulations composed of ALC-0315, DOPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000 were prepared and evaluated in terms of physicochemical properties, mRNA encapsulation, platelet activation, and transfection efficiency. We found that varying the DOPC/cholesterol ratio was associated with differences in nanoparticle morphology, platelet responses, and delivery efficiency, with F3 showing the highest reporter expression among the five formulations tested. The optimized formulation enabled efficient expression of functional superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) mRNA in platelets without inducing significant activation. Functional studies showed that SOD2 overexpression markedly reduced mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and total ROS levels while preserving platelet ultrastructure and aggregation function. This study establishes a platelet-compatible LNP platform for functional mRNA delivery and provides new insights into the structure-activity relationship of LNP formulations in platelet gene delivery.

abstract: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) associate with RNAs in intricate ribonucleoprotein complexes and regulate various aspects of RNA life cycle and, by extension, cell functions. Despite their significance, elucidating the functional contributions of specific RNA-RBP binding events, particularly in long-term phenotypic assays, remains challenging. Here, we harness the specificity of CRISPR/dCas13 to interfere with specific RNA-RBP interactions. We apply this methodology to GA-rich mRNA localization elements which recruit the RNA-binding protein CNBP and serve as platforms for the assembly of mRNA trafficking complexes. We show that dCas13/gRNA binds to target transcripts in a highly specific manner and interferes with CNBP recruitment leading to altered target mRNA localization and cell motility, consistent with the function of the targeted mRNAs. We describe optimizations and considerations for the stable implementation of this system. We further use it to show that interfering with the localization of the GA-containing NET1 mRNA reduces cancer cell invasiveness and metastatic lung colonization. These data reveal a potential role for mRNA localization in oncogenic progression and illustrate how this CRISPR-based system can be used for long-term functional investigations of RNA-RBP interactions in vivo.

abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Chemotherapy-induced oral mucositis involves epithelial injury, inflammation, delayed mucosal repair, and microbial dysbiosis. This study investigated whether live Streptococcus salivarius K12 and a K12-derived bacterial extracellular vesicle (BEV) preparation alleviate 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)-associated oral mucosal injury.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: K12-derived BEVs were isolated and characterized, and live K12 or the BEV preparation was administered orally to male mice. The model combined systemic 5-FU exposure with local acetic acid-induced tongue injury. Oral mucosal repair, inflammatory transcript expression, and oral and fecal microbiota were evaluated.
RESULTS: Both interventions promoted wound healing and increased epithelial thickness and collagen deposition compared with the 5-FU group. In tongue tissue, live K12 significantly reduced Tnf and Il6 mRNA expression relative to the 5-FU group, whereas the reduction in Il1b was not statistically significant. The BEV preparation significantly reduced all three transcripts relative to the 5-FU group. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed group-associated variation in oral and fecal microbial community structure. K12 and BEV treatment were associated with different descriptive patterns of microbial composition. Under the non-dose-matched regimens tested, the BEV preparation produced greater improvements than live K12 in selected repair- and inflammation-related outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support further investigation of K12-derived BEV preparations as a potential cell-free intervention for chemotherapy-associated oral mucosal injury.

abstract: Intranasal administration is a promising non-invasive approach for the potential nose-to-brain (N2B) delivery of messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics; however, developing nasal spray systems for this purpose requires consideration of regional nasal deposition and the preservation of lipid nanoparticle (LNP) integrity during spray actuation. Although the performance of mechanical nasal spray pumps depends strongly on their mode of actuation, the effects of actuation conditions on regional nasal deposition and mRNA-LNP stability have rarely been evaluated concurrently. Here, a mechanical nasal spray device was evaluated at three spring compression forces (4.8, 8.0, and 11.2 N) and actuation speeds of 80-180 mm/s. Plume geometry, spray pattern, droplet size distribution, and single-actuation content and volume were characterized, followed by regional deposition analysis in an in vitro three-dimensional nasal cast. A higher compression force significantly increased the relative stained area in the superior-turbinate region of the cast, an anatomical region potentially relevant to N2B transport, whereas increasing the actuation speed shifted the stained-area distribution toward the middle turbinate. Following actuation of the mRNA-LNPs, encapsulation efficiency significantly decreased under all conditions and was a more sensitive indicator of instability than particle size, indicating that device actuation alone did not preserve LNP integrity. Incorporating polymeric excipients suppressed actuation-induced aggregation. Among these excipients, poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) was selected as a representative polymer for further spray and deposition characterization. The addition of 0.5% PVA increased droplet size without significantly altering plume geometry and significantly increased the relative stained area in the middle turbinate. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that nasal spray actuation and formulation both govern regional nasal deposition and mRNA-LNP stability, underscoring the need to co-optimize device performance and formulation when developing nasal spray systems intended for N2B delivery of mRNA-LNPs. Epithelial transport, neuronal uptake, brain distribution, and mRNA expression were not evaluated; therefore, the observed deposition patterns do not establish N2B delivery or biological activity.

abstract: Aberrant glycosylation reshapes tumour-host communication through glycan-protein interactions, driving immune evasion, invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. These interactions regulate signalling between tumour cells and their microenvironment, influencing disease progression and clinical outcomes. This review summarises the structural basis of glycan recognition and its functional roles in tumour progression, with emphasis on glycan-lectin interactions, immune modulation, extracellular matrix remodelling, and angiogenesis. We further discuss recent advances in glycan-based biomarkers, glycoproteomic profiling, glycomimetic therapeutics, glycan-targeted antibodies, and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence-assisted glycomics and CRISPR-based glycoengineering. Collectively, these advances highlight the translational potential of glycan-protein interactions for improving cancer diagnosis, patient stratification, and the development of precision therapies targeting tumour-associated glycosylation.

title: Glycan-Protein Interactions in Tumour Progression, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Targeting.

abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most frequently acquired sexually transmitted infection. The E6 and E7 oncoproteins of HPV mainly contribute to the development of cancerous lesions by dysregulating the host p53 and pRb tumour suppressor pathways, respectively. Although prophylactic vaccines are available for HPV infection, they are ineffective for established HPV infections. Despite significant advances in surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapies, recurrent, metastatic, and treatment-resistant HPV-associated cancers continue to present substantial clinical challenges, highlighting the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies.As the E6 and E7 viral oncoproteins are key drivers of HPV-positive cancer pathogenesis, targeting these proteins represents a rational approach for developing new therapies. Gene therapy is currently studied extensively as a potential strategy for cancer regression. RNA interference technology and CRISPR approaches are highly effective in downregulating the expression of viral oncoproteins. In most cancer types, tumour suppressor proteins are frequently mutated; however, in HPV-induced cancers, they typically remain wild type. Hence, increasing the bioavailability of tumour suppressor proteins is a therapeutic option. CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) is a CRISPR system variant in which catalytically inactive Cas9 (dcas9) is fused with a transcriptional activator to induce gene expression. Unlike CRISPR, CRISPRa increases the expression of the targeted gene without genomic modifications. Although there are few strategies available to increase the expression of tumour suppressor proteins, CRISPRa has gained a major focus as an effective and promising strategy. There is potential to develop CRISPRa as a future therapeutic intervention to treat HPV induced cancers combined with other treatment modalities.

abstract: Multiplex determination of pathogens is crucial for precise medical treatment of infectious diseases. To address this challenge, here we propose a CRISPR/Cas-assisted microfluidic multiplex sensing platform (CAMMSP) based on a nucleic acid amplification-free, universal, and modular sensing strategy. This strategy leverages the synergistic action of Cas12a and nanoporous materials to construct a target-responsive indicator release/enrichment system and achieve cascade signal amplification without nucleic acid amplification. By virtue of the programmability of the CRISPR system, this strategy is readily extended to different targets by replacing crRNA only. With the aid of a spatially divisional microfluidic platform, four common reproductive tract pathogens were synchronously detected as a proof-of-concept. The signal property of the methylene blue indicator was utilized to achieve electrochemical and optical signal cross-validation, guaranteeing the detection reliability at the readout level and offering flexible options for different scenarios. The developed CAMMSP exhibits broad linear ranges across 6 orders of magnitude and sub-femtomolar detection limits, with outstanding specificity in complex samples. Clinical sample analysis further validates its potential for practical applications, establishing a promising laboratory proof-of-concept and reliable technical foundation for developing multiplex point-of-care testing devices.

title: Multiplex Determination of Pathogens via a Dual-Mode Microfluidic Platform Integrated with a Universal Sensing Strategy.

abstract: Sensitive and reliable quantification of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA is important for monitoring viral replication and therapeutic response. Electrochemical (EC) sensing offers simple quantitative readout, but resolving current changes at low target concentrations remains challenging. Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS), in contrast, provides signal amplification but generally requires specialized optical instrumentation and may suffer from matrix interference. To accommodate different analytical requirements, we developed a CRISPR/Cas12a-triggered dual-mode EC/SERS biosensing platform. This platform integrates a conductive/plasmonic gold nanoparticles (Au NPs)/copper(II)-2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene (Cu3(HHTP)2)/indium tin oxide (ITO) interface with a CRISPR-responsive DNA hydrogel. The hydrogel serves as a target-responsive interfacial gate, with Cas12a-mediated cleavage regulating electrode accessibility to facilitate EC transduction and promote plasmonic coupling between SERS tags and Au NPs. Ag@Au nanocubes functionalized with 4-mercaptobenzonitrile were employed as SERS tags, providing a characteristic CN signal at 2228 cm-1 in the Raman-silent region. The EC mode exhibited a linear response to the logarithm of HBV DNA concentration from 100 fM to 10 nM, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 17.1 fM. The SERS mode was evaluated in parallel on a separate, identically prepared hydrogel-modified electrode, yielding a linear range of 5 fM to 1 nM and an LOD of 0.143 fM. This platform combines the operational simplicity and quantitative capability of EC sensing with the high sensitivity of SERS detection, providing complementary readout options for different HBV DNA testing requirements.

title: CRISPR/Cas12a-Triggered Dual-Mode Electrochemical and Raman-Silent Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering Biosensing for Sensitive HBV DNA Detection.

abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a zoonotic pathogen with high mortality and limited therapeutic options, and listed as a priority pathogen in the WHO's R&D Blueprint. Using a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen, we identified Arsenical pump-driving ATPase protein (ASNA-1/TRC40) as a novel host factor required for CCHFV infection. Knockout of ASNA-1 leads to a significant inhibition of viral replication across multiple clinical isolates of CCHFV, spanning diverse geographic clades. Furthermore, the small-molecule inhibitor Retro-2.1, which targets ASNA-1/TRC40 in the Transmembrane Domain Recognition Complex (TRC) pathway, potently inhibits CCHFV replication without significant cytotoxicity. Our findings demonstrate that ASNA-1 is essential for the CCHFV life cycle and establish the ASNA-1/TRC40 pathway as a viable, broad-spectrum target for antiviral intervention against this neglected and lethal human pathogen.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 Knockout Screen Identifies "Arsenical Pump-Driving ATPase Protein" as a Novel Host Factor Supporting Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus Infection.

abstract: Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) at an early stage of transcription initiation. Fidaxomicin is used for treating Clostridioides difficile infections and has demonstrated in vitro efficacy against drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Fidaxomicin derivatives are currently the focus of extensive research to develop novel antibacterial agents. Previous studies showed that region 3.2 of the RNAP primary σ factor and the mycobacterial transcriptional activator RbpA modulate fidaxomicin potency through poorly understood mechanisms. Moreover, the impact of the structurally distinct extracytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors on fidaxomicin potency has never been explored. Here, using DNA scaffold-based in vitro transcription assays, we found that RbpA-dependent primary σ factors from Mtb enhance fidaxomicin potency, whereas ECF σ factors render Mtb RNAP resistant to fidaxomicin. Contrary to the prevailing assumptions, RbpA has only a marginal effect on fidaxomicin potency. Our structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations support a model in which ECF σ factors obstruct fidaxomicin binding by changing the configuration of the RNAP RNA channel. Conversely, the direct interaction between fidaxomicin and RbpA-dependent primary σ factors does not affect drug binding. Our findings identify the σ factor as a key modulator of fidaxomicin potency and provide a framework to explore σ factor structural diversity for designing pathogen-specific fidaxomicin analogs. Moreover, these results highlight fundamental mechanistic differences between the modes of action of housekeeping and ECF σ factors during transcription initiation.

title: The σ subunit identity, rather than RbpA, is the major determinant of M. tuberculosis RNA polymerase sensitivity to fidaxomicin.

abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a heritable cardiac disorder commonly linked to alterations in desmosomal proteins. While desmosomal dysfunction is a recognized pathogenic mechanism, the early molecular remodeling that precedes clinical manifestations remains unclear. Here we used a mouse model with inducible cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pkp2 (encoding plakophilin-2) and performed time-resolved mass spectrometry-based proteomics to map disease progression from early PKP2 loss to structural remodeling. Molecular changes preceded phenotypic abnormalities, and spatial asymmetry was evident, with earlier and more pronounced proteome remodeling in the right ventricle despite comparable PKP2 depletion in both ventricles. Downregulation of protein networks spanning desmosomes, sarcomeres and mitochondria suggests their functional coupling, with mitochondrial remodeling emerging as an early and progressively worsening feature. Intervention with honokiol attenuated changes across the major protein networks, highlighting mitochondrial pathways as promising therapeutic targets and honokiol as a potential strategy to delay arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy progression. Our findings provide critical insights into the concealed stage of disease progression and identify molecular targets for early intervention.

abstract: Ischemia-reperfusion (I-R) injury is a major complication in liver transplantation and a primary driver of graft rejection lacking effective therapeutic interventions. To identify proteins whose disruption confers resistance against I-R damage, a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen was performed in AML12 hepatocytes. Bioinformatic analysis of the screen revealed an enrichment of knockouts involved in ferroptosis and protein synthesis. While initial rescue by the lysosomotropic iron chelator deferoxamine aligned with the screen findings regarding ferroptosis, subsequent validation proved that neither iron nor lipid peroxidation-the sine qua non of ferroptosis-is necessary for cell death. Rather, the mechanism requires lysosomal function during the ischemic phase. It proceeds without DNA damage, autophagy, or lysosomal breakdown. This cell death pathway remains functional across diverse models, including ferroptosis-resistant HepG2 and ferroptosis-sensitive HT1080 cells. Protection by deferoxamine and chloroquine, combined with insensitivity to ferrostatin-1, defines a distinct pharmacologic profile that differentiates this mechanism from previously known cell death routes. Overall, this study establishes the existence of a novel cell death mechanism in ischemia-reperfusion.

abstract: Reticuloendotheliosis virus (REV) is an immunosuppressive and oncogenic pathogen that causes substantial economic losses in poultry production. In the absence of commercial vaccines and specific therapeutic agents against REV, early and accurate detection is essential for REV control and eradication. In this study, a visual RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay was established for REV detection based on a conserved 552-bp region of the pol gene. RAA primers and crRNA were screened, and the reaction conditions were systematically optimized. The assay was completed at 37 °C with 20min of RAA amplification and 40min of Cas12a reaction, and results were read visually under blue/UV light. The limit of detection was 10 copies/μL. The assay showed no cross-reactivity with other common avian pathogens and exhibited good repeatability. When 90 clinical samples were tested, the RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay detected 50 positive samples (55.55%), whereas qPCR detected 43 positive samples (47.77%). The overall agreement was 85.56% (77/90), with a positive agreement of 93.02% (40/43), a negative agreement of 78.72% (37/47), and a Cohen's kappa of 0.713. These results indicate that the RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay is a rapid, specific, and visual method for REV detection and provides a complementary tool for REV screening, although further validation with live birds and other sample types is required.
